b0640610b4ecd08c: <!--kg-card-end: html--> As the Treasury Department dealt with the fallout of a hack that took down some of its services, its Chief Information Officer was pushing updates to Legatum, his vibe coded Civilization clone.

Sam Corcos is the cofounder of the A16z-backed glucose monitoring health startup called Levels; he became the Treasury Department’s Chief Information Officer as a DOGE hire near the beginning of Trump’s second term, and has been a leading AI evangelist within the administration since. Corcos’s department is in charge of cybersecurity for the Treasury Department, and so it is possibly concerning that while the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is dealing with a “cybersecurity incident” that has taken a critical bank compliance reporting panel down, he has been actively pushing balance patches, new theme music for the Aztec faction, and critical tweaks to the in-game player assistance tooltips for Legatum, his vibe-coded “turn-based strategy game in the tradition of Civilization VI.”

Legatum is similar to Civilization VI “on purpose,” according to a readme on Corcos’s Github. “If you have played Civilization VI you already know the basics: found cities, pick research, queue production, fight on hexes […] Legatum is built largely with AI coding agents [both Claude and OpenAI’s Codex], and all of its art is AI-generated. Most of the art comes from OpenAI's image models through ChatGPT.”

Legatum is also open source, and has been getting updated in real time while I am writing this article and after a notice went up on the FinCEN website that said it was “investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.”

While newer AI models can do a lot on their own and can often work for hours or days without much human intervention, shoddy or lazy prompting by Corcos has resulted in a situation where Claude is pushing updates that come as the result of direct feedback from Corcos about improvements that can be made to the game. Some of the most recent updates include direct quotes from Corcos about how he’s feeling about the game, indicating that he is actively involved in its development.

One of the most recent updates, pushed after the FinCEN hack, includes, for example, a new special unit for Egypt, which came at the explicit direction of Corcos. “I like Chariot archers for egypt, their current special unit is lame,” Corcos told Claude. That update was pushed while a Treasury Department website displayed a warning noting that “as a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.”

“FinCEN is working diligently to return all systems to normal operations as soon as possible,” FinCEN added. Luckily, Legatum players will not have to wait any longer for more faction-appropriate music as Corcos and his AI have been working diligently to improve the game’s “production value,” according to a Github commit pushed after midnight on Wednesday. This new update includes “Music by era, the Aztecs' own music, the sea, and gunpowder-age battle sounds.”

The federal government has suffered a series of high-profile outages and hacks in recent weeks; the FinCEN hack followed earlier hacks at the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence that were carried out by hackers using the Artex artificial intelligence hacking tool, according to the New York Times. In addition to his work as a hobbyist game vibecoder and Treasury CIO, Corcos was involved in several General Services Administration projects, including one at Login.gov, which we previously reported was to have AI integrated throughout.

Corcos previously seized control of several U.S. government Github repositories and was accused earlier this fall of deleting comments that pointed out regulatory compliance violations associated with the way the US Web Design System was attempting to automate accessibility testing. At the time I’m writing this, Corcos has not deleted a user-reported issue with Legatum that states “treasury CIO is too busy vibe coding instead of doing his job.” That issue is full of people clowning on Corcos.

Earlier this fall, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Corcos he could no longer work on AI policy after he held several unauthorized meetings with OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Politico. In those meetings, “Corcos portrayed himself as an industry ally and warned that other government officials, reacting to fears over the latest AI models, were attempting to impose a burdensome licensing regime that would hamper innovation.” Politico did not report on whether Corcos had sought feedback from OpenAI and Anthropic on Legatum, which “is not affiliated with, endorsed by or derived from Sid Meier’s Civilization,” a notice on its GitHub reads.

Crucially, players can play Legatum in a web browser: “Nothing to install.” Something you can’t do in a web browser, at the moment, is reliably file certain compliance documents about the Banking Secrecy Act with the Treasury Department; “FinCEN is extending deadlines for filers impacted by the disruption,” it said. I did play Legatum for several minutes in my web browser but then got bored and decided to go searching through Corcos’s GitHub instead.

Corcos’s most recent tweet reads “I believe it is reasonable to ask employees what they are working on,” in response to the news that some federal workers would be ordered to send updates about what they are working on. Corcos, it seems, has been working on making sure that the walls in Legatum are better in the mid-to-late game and to fix graphical glitches with walls: “feels like we could do better,” he told Claude.
The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment.
f5bb5e8a9ad3e428: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

4080b1864c3dc749: NOVEMBER 25 — The recent controversy surrounding the Bahasa Melayu paper in the 2026 Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) examination, particularly on penjodoh bilangan, should concern us beyond the examination hall. Reports of some candidates struggling to answer questions on a grammatical concept introduced during primary education, and allegedly questioning its relevance to everyday life, invite a much larger discussion about our relationship with language.

Have we reached a point where we expect our language to become simpler because we are no longer willing to master its complexities? It is not the inability to answer an examination question that worries me most. Students make mistakes, and that is part of learning. What is more troubling is the attitude that something is no longer worth learning simply because we rarely use it.

Every language carries the intellectual, cultural and historical wealth of its community. Our mother tongue connects us to our ancestors, traditions, values and ways of understanding the world. When we lose command of a language, we risk losing access to generations of accumulated wisdom. In Bahasa Melayu, expressions such as sehelai daun, seutas tali, sekuntum bunga and sebilah pisau reflect the precision and richness of the language. These distinctions demonstrate how generations before us observed, understood and categorised their surroundings. Reducing language to what is convenient is like reducing mathematics to what a calculator can do. The same applies to Mandarin, Tamil, Iban, Kadazandusun and other languages spoken across Malaysia. Each deserves preservation, appreciation and intellectual respect. Bahasa Melayu, meanwhile, carries the additional responsibility of being our national language and a shared means of communication across ethnic and cultural boundaries.

Today's younger generation has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to acquire new vocabulary from social media, online gaming and popular culture. Words such as delulu, rizz, slay, cringe and no cap enter their vocabulary almost effortlessly. Yet, why should learning penjodoh bilangan, peribahasa or proper sentence structures suddenly be considered an unreasonable academic burden? Perhaps the problem is not our capacity to learn languages, but what we choose to value.

There is nothing wrong with embracing contemporary expressions, mixing languages in informal conversations or mastering English and other international languages. Language naturally evolves. However, linguistic evolution should enrich our vocabulary, not impoverish it. Being globally competent should never require us to become linguistically disconnected from our own roots. It would be unfair to place the entire blame on young people. Parents, teachers, educational institutions, media organisations and society at large must examine the linguistic environment we have created. How often do parents encourage their children to read literature in their mother tongue? How frequently do schools take language learning beyond textbooks and examination exercises? Do universities provide sufficient opportunities for students to engage in intellectual discussions in Bahasa Melayu?

We cannot demand linguistic excellence from children when adults themselves treat proper language use as an inconvenience. Schools must make language come alive through storytelling, theatre, debates, creative writing, traditional games and meaningful conversations. Students must experience language as something they can live with, create with and take pride in, rather than merely memorise for examinations.

To our young Malaysians, master English. Learn Mandarin, Arabic, Japanese, Korean or any other language that opens doors to the world. Be ambitious, multilingual and internationally competitive but never allow your pursuit of global recognition to come at the expense of your linguistic identity. Do not mistake unfamiliarity for irrelevance. Do not dismiss knowledge simply because it demands effort. And do not wear linguistic ignorance as a badge of modernity.

The recent SPM controversy should not become an opportunity to ridicule our young people. Instead, it should become a moment of national reflection. An examination may determine how many marks a student loses for an incorrect answer. But when an entire generation begins to question the value of its linguistic heritage, what we stand to lose is far greater than a few marks.
A language does not disappear because its people can no longer speak it. It begins to disappear when its people no longer believe it is worth mastering.
* Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Noor Abdul Aziz and Assoc Prof Dr Mohd Isha Awang are from the School of Education, Universiti Utara Malaysia.
* * This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.

bd5728b34d4f0866: London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.
A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.
AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically.
Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go.

The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected.
Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations.

The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases."
Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated.
Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues.
Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected.
Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual.
The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details.
Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information.
Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded.

"The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest.
"Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

55123006818679b1: KUANTAN, Nov 25 — Pahang Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Wan Rosdy Wan Ismail today said he had no plans to dissolve the State Legislative Assembly (DUN) to pave the way for a state election.
“There are no plans as of today,” he said briefly at the Pahang State Legislative Assembly sitting at Wisma Sri Pahang here.

He was responding to a question from Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man (PN-Cheka), who wanted to know whether the Pahang DUN would be dissolved following remarks by several assemblymen suggesting that the current sitting could be their last.

Tuan Ibrahim raised the question while interjecting during the debate on the Pahang 2027 Budget by Datuk Seri Shafik Fauzan Sharif (BN-Inderapura), who had described the sitting as his ‘final days’ as the Inderapura assemblyman after 22 years in the post since 2004.
Shafik Fauzan also said he had no intention of defending the Inderapura state seat in the next general election (GE16).
Meanwhile, when met by reporters, Tuan Ibrahim said there had been no formal discussions so far on cooperation with Pahang Barisan Nasional (BN).
“Not yet. We are sounding them out first. PAS leaders in each state have been instructed to hold meetings at all levels to explore ways to advance the agenda of unity of the ummah,” he said.

611e7b7f6425c133: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 25 — Genting Plantations Bhd posted a higher net profit of RM93.31 million in third quarter ended September 30, 2026 (3Q 2026), compared to RM86.50 million in the same period last year.

In a Bursa Malaysia filing today, it said revenue rose to RM938.45 million in 3Q 2026 from RM846.95 million previously, driven by higher fresh fruit bunch (FFB) production and improved sales volumes in the downstream manufacturing segment.

“FFB production in 3Q 2026 and year-to-date (YTD) 2026 increased year-on-year, mainly attributable to higher cropping trends across certain estates within the group and recovery following the unusually heavy rainfall and flooding experienced in 2025,” it said.

For the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026 (9M 2026), the company recorded a lower net profit of RM302.29 million against RM340.33 million in the same period last year, while revenue increased to RM2.65 billion from RM2.33 billion previously.

In a separate statement, Genting Plantations said the group achieved crude palm oil prices of RM3,881 per metric tonne (mt) and RM3,762 per mt in 3Q 2026 and YTD 2026, respectively. Palm kernel price stood at RM3,344 per mt and RM3,334 per mt in 3Q 2026 and YTD 2026, respectively.

On its prospects, the group said its performance for the remainder of the year would depend largely on its core plantation segment, which is principally influenced by movements in palm product prices and FFB production.

“The group expects palm oil prices to remain under some near-term downward pressure, mainly due to higher palm oil production and elevated stock levels, coupled with the recent correction in crude oil prices.

“Nevertheless, the current price weakness is expected to be temporary and partly mitigated by stronger Indonesian biodiesel demand, as well as the potential impact of the severe El Niño phenomenon experienced recently, which is expected to constrain industry-wide palm oil production for the next two years,” it said.

Genting Plantations expects the effects of the severe El Niño phenomenon to begin setting in during the remaining months of the year, with some moderation in FFB production expected towards the year-end.

Nevertheless, the progression of existing mature areas into higher-yielding age profiles across some estates is expected to provide some support to production and partially mitigate the impact, it added. — Bernama

e08961cf23cd09d1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 25 — A private university student pleaded not guilty in the Magistrate’s Court today to a charge of reckless driving that resulted in the death of a retired military personnel on Jalan Jelatek here last Saturday.
The accused, a 32-year-old Libyan national, Ali Abdul Rahman Mahmoud Elmaki, entered his plea after the charge was read to him in English before Magistrate Amalina Johar.

According to the charge, the man allegedly drove a Proton Saga recklessly and dangerously, causing the death of 43-year-old Mohd Hairezam Omar on Jalan Jelatek from the direction of Wangsa Maju towards Taman Keramat at 1 am on Nov 21.

The charge is brought under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987, which carries a maximum fine of RM50,000 or imprisonment for up to 10 years. Additionally, a conviction under this section would result in an endorsement on the offender’s driving license.
Deputy Public Prosecutor Mohamad Fadhly Mohd Zamry objected to the granting of bail, citing the fact that the accused is a foreign national and that the offence committed is of a serious nature.
“However, should the court choose to exercise its discretion to grant bail under Section 388 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the prosecution proposes bail at RM70,000 with two Malaysian sureties.

“The prosecution also requests additional conditions: that the accused’s passport be surrendered to the court, that he reports to the nearest police station at least once a month, and that he is prohibited from using his driving license until the conclusion of the case. I request that the court consider these conditions should bail be granted, given that the accused is a foreign national and poses a flight risk,” said Mohamad Fadhly.

Defence counsel K. Ramalingam, representing the accused, requested a lower bail amount around RM10,000 on the grounds that his client is a Master’s degree student who is scheduled to sit for examinations next month.
“The accused resides in Malaysia with his wife and has a permanent address on Jalan Ampang. He is also prepared to accept all additional conditions requested by the prosecution,” he said.

The court subsequently granted bail at RM17,000 with two Malaysian sureties, subject to additional conditions that the accused must surrender his passport to the court, report to a nearby police station once a month, and have his driver’s license suspended until the conclusion of the case.
The court has set January 28 of next year for the next mention of the case.

Previously, media reports indicated that the victim, who was riding a motorcycle from the direction of Taman Keramat toward Setiawangsa, was struck by a car driven by a Libyan national coming from the direction of Wangsa Maju, who had failed to stop at a red traffic light.
The victim, who sustained severe injuries, was pronounced dead at the scene, while alcohol and urine screening tests conducted on the driver returned negative results. — Bernama
75137a46df95c53c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 25 — Bursa Malaysia Securities Bhd has publicly reprimanded RHB Investment Bank Bhd (RHB IB), the recognised principal adviser for Capital A Bhd, for breaching the Bursa Malaysia Securities Main Market Listing Requirements (Main LR).

In a statement, Bursa Malaysia said that under Breach 1, RHB IB was publicly reprimanded for breach of the provisions of the Main LR for failing to ensure that there was at least 10 market days’ notice of the books closing date (BCD).

It said the BCD was fixed on December 3, 2025, for the adjustments to the conversion price and ratio of 7-Year redeemable convertible unsecured Islamic debt securities 2021/2028 (RCUIDS) and the exercise price of warrants 2021/2028 (warrants) in the company arising from the distribution announced on April 25, 2024.

It said that for Breach 2, RHB IB was publicly reprimanded for breaching the provisions of the Main LR for failing to ensure the distribution announced on April 25, 2024, was completed within one month from the BCD on or before January 2, 2026.

Bursa Malaysia said the finding of breach and imposition of the public reprimand on RHB IB were made pursuant to paragraph 16.19 of the Main LR, upon completion of due process after taking into consideration all facts and circumstances of the matter.

This included the materiality of the breaches, RHB IB’s roles and responsibilities as a recognised principal adviser, and the fact that RHB IB had previously committed breaches of the listing requirements, it said.

“Bursa Malaysia Securities views the contraventions seriously as the timely announcement of the BCD and timely completion of the distribution are of paramount importance in ensuring an orderly and fair market for securities traded on Bursa Malaysia Securities and maintaining market integrity and investor confidence,” it said.

On April 25, 2024, RHB IB, on behalf of the company, announced various corporate proposals, including the proposed distribution of 1.69 billion new ordinary shares in AirAsia X Bhd to the company’s entitled shareholders.
“The distribution gave rise to adjustments to the conversion price and ratio of the RCUIDS and the exercise price of the warrants (adjustments).

“On November 19, 2025, RHB IB submitted an announcement on behalf of the company stating that the BCD for the distribution had been fixed on December 3, 2025. However, the BCD for the adjustments was not announced on the same day,” it said.

The exchange said it was only on Nov 27, 2025, following Bursa Malaysia Securities’ engagement, that RHB IB announced on behalf of the company that the BCD for the adjustments had been fixed on December 3, 2025.
As a result, it said only four market days’ notice was given of the BCD instead of the minimum 10 market days’ notice required under paragraph 9.19(1) of the Main LR.
“Further, pursuant to paragraph 9.19(2)(a)(ii) of the Main LR, the distribution was required to be completed within one month from the BCD of December 3, 2025, that is, by Jan 2, 2026.
“However, the distribution was only completed on January 19, 2026, 11 market days after the prescribed deadline,” it said.
The delay affected market integrity, as investors would have traded based on the company’s announcement on November 19, 2025, it said.

“While the company’s securities traded ex-distribution from Dec 2, 2025, at an adjusted reference price of RM0.245, reducing the company’s market capitalisation by approximately RM2.646 billion or 71.16 per cent, shareholders did not receive the distribution shares until January 19, 2026,” it added. — Bernama
c45f0469d579113d: JERUSALEM, Nov 25 — Amnesty International accused Israel on Wednesday of imposing measures that prevented births in Gaza, while its chief called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate the possible “commission of genocide”.

In a report published Wednesday on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, Amnesty paints a bleak picture of the consequences of the war that began in October 2023 on the physical, mental and reproductive health of women in Gaza.

Since then, “Israel’s actions have prevented access to fertility treatment and contributed to pregnancy complications, including miscarriage and stillbirth,” Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard said at a press conference.
The report expresses “serious concerns that this outcome was intentional”, but acknowledges that it is “not in a position to conclude this categorically”.
Contacted by AFP, COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body in charge of civilian matters in the Palestinian territories, accused Amnesty of “echoing Hamas’s false narratives”.

It said more than 27,000 tonnes of medical equipment and medicine have entered Gaza since a US-brokered ceasefire began in October 2025 and that 35 hospitals were operational, including “women’s health and fertility facilities”.
Israel’s foreign ministry said the report “reads like a political pamphlet masquerading as human rights research… levelling outrageous accusations against Israel that it admits it cannot prove.”
The report details cases of women and girls killed or injured in Israeli attacks while seeking medical care or while in maternity wards in Gaza.
Many women went through pregnancy or tended to their newborns despite their injuries under relentless bombardment, the report says.
Shortages of medical equipment have also compromised pregnancy monitoring, obstetric and postnatal care, as well as the diagnosis of complications, according to Amnesty.
It added that shortages of anaesthetics and medicines needed to treat haemorrhaging during childbirth have sometimes had fatal consequences.
Amnesty attributed the shortages to Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, which “contribute to rising maternal and neonatal mortality”.

In light of these conclusions, Callamard called on the ICC to “consider the commission of genocide by Israeli officials since October 2023” and to include in its investigation “gender-based crimes and reproductive harms”.

“Measures intended to prevent births” within a group constitute an act of genocide when undertaken with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part,” that group, according to Article II of the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
No treatment available

Among the 228 interviews conducted for the report, two paramedics told Amnesty of two incidents that occurred in early 2026, a few hundred metres from the so-called Yellow Line demarcating the area under Israeli control in the Gaza Strip.
In both cases, a woman about to give birth and the ambulance dispatched to collect her came under fire, according to their testimony.
The report also cites the case of a 20-day-old infant who died in 2025 from an infection contracted after sharing an incubator with another sick baby.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war sparked by Hamas’s unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The ministry also reported a roughly 41 percent drop in the number of live births in the first half of 2025 compared with 2022. The UN also recorded a decline in the number of deliveries in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period the previous year.

The NGO also said it has “found evidence” of the use of hospitals “by Palestinian armed groups”, notably to hold hostages or for the “torture of Palestinians”, but has found no evidence supporting Israeli accusations of their use as Hamas command centres.
Amnesty also said that before the war, Gaza had at least nine clinics offering in vitro fertilisation (IVF) but none now provide these treatments.
“Thousands of stored embryos, sperm and eggs were destroyed,” it said. — AFP
bfae15a47271a721: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 25 — Residents in low-lying areas and near the coast have been advised to increase their level of preparedness following the forecast of high tides, rain and thunderstorms in most areas of the state until Friday (Nov 27).

Penang Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM) director Mohamad Shoki Hamzah said the public should take note of the high and low tide schedule for George Town and Penang Port, particularly those living in flood-prone areas.

c1308a0df1564ed0: TAIPING, Nov 25 — A female teenager was brought before the Magistrate’s Court here today on a charge of murdering her newborn baby girl by stabbing the infant last week.
Nurul Iman Najiha Abdullah, 19, nodded in understanding when the charge against her was read out before Magistrate R. Prabakaran.
However, no plea was recorded from the accused on the murder charge as the case falls under the jurisdiction of the High Court.

Nurul Iman Najiha was charged with murdering a baby girl, who was her biological child, in an oil palm area behind a house in Kampung Panchor, Pantai Remis, in the Larut, Matang and Selama district, between Nov 14 and 16.

The charge was framed under Section 302 of the Penal Code, which carries the death penalty or imprisonment of not less than 30 years and not exceeding 40 years, and if not sentenced to death, shall also be punished with whipping of not less than 12 strokes, upon conviction.

Meanwhile, in a separate charge, Nurul Iman Najiha and her boyfriend, Mohamad Aidil Eikmal, 19, were jointly charged with common intention to conceal the birth of the baby girl by secretly burying the infant’s body at the same location and dates.
They were charged under Section 318 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34 of the same code, which provides for a maximum prison sentence of two years, or a fine, or both, upon conviction.
Mohamad Aidil pleaded guilty to the charge, while Nurul Iman Najiha pleaded not guilty.
Deputy Public Prosecutor Farihah Adilah Faizal requested bail at RM50,000 with one surety for each accused, while no bail was offered for the murder charge faced by Nurul Iman Najiha.

Meanwhile, counsel from the National Legal Aid Foundation (YBGK) Nurul Hanis Mohd Zaini, representing both accused, appealed for lower bail as this was their first offence and the couple worked as an eatery assistant and a construction labourer respectively.
“Nurul Iman Najiha also has mental health issues but has never sought treatment,” the lawyer said.

The court then set bail at RM5,000 with two sureties for each accused and fixed Jan 4 for re-mention of the case for Nurul Iman Najiha to appoint a lawyer, as well as for a social report from the Social Welfare Department for Mohamad Aidil before sentencing him.
On Nov 19, Perak Police Chief Datuk Mohd Alwi Zainal Abidin said a newborn baby girl died after allegedly being stabbed by her biological mother in an incident in Pantai Remis on Nov 14.
He said preliminary investigations found that the 19-year-old teenager committed the act at her home before contacting her boyfriend to help bury the baby’s body behind the house. — Bernama
83de6d15a1a7e49c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 25 — Retail prices of RON97, unsubsidised RON95 and unsubsidised diesel will all fall by 25 sen per litre from Nov 26 to Dec 2.

The Finance Ministry (MOF) said today that under the Automatic Pricing Mechanism (APM) formula, RON97 will drop from RM4.00 to RM3.75 per litre, while unsubsidised RON95 will fall from RM3.72 to RM3.47 per litre.
The retail price of unsubsidised diesel will fall from RM4.72 to RM4.47 per litre.
According to MOF, refined petroleum product prices in regional markets moderated during the APM calculation period, easing price pressure in the international petroleum market.
“At the same time, prospects of higher global crude oil supply also contributed to lower world oil prices. However, refined petroleum supplies still face constraints in certain markets.

“Geopolitical uncertainty and risks of petroleum delivery disruptions could still affect global supply. Therefore, world oil prices are expected to continue fluctuating in the near term,” the statement said.

Meanwhile, it said the Madani government remains committed to protecting the people and businesses through targeted fuel subsidies under Budi Madani, with nearly RM40 billion allocated for fuel subsidies next year to ease cost-of-living pressures.

Under Budi95, eligible recipients will continue paying RM1.99 per litre for RON95 compared with the unsubsidised price of RM3.47 per litre, with the government subsidising RM1.48 per litre, or 43 per cent of the unsubsidised price.

e3cce5e7b1692e2b: RIYADH, Nov 25 — The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said Wednesday it had struck Yemen’s key port city of Hodeida, while the Iran-backed group threatened to retaliate as the conflict further escalated.
The Houthis also claimed responsibility for attacks a day earlier on the Saudi capital that struck the tallest tower in its financial district, wounding 11.
In recent weeks the group has launched a barrage at Saudi targets including the financial district, airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.

The Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi-held areas of Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government, which has been battling the Houthis for territory since a civil war reignited in July.
“We targeted operational capabilities at the port of Hodeida,” the coalition posted to X on Wednesday, having earlier warned civilians to evacuate.
Hodeidah is under Houthi control and is a key entry point for goods into Yemeni territory held by the group.
Houthi media outlet Almasirah confirmed Hodeida had been targeted but did not provide details. No casualties or injuries were reported.
Almasirah added that Saudi forces had also attacked the area’s international airport.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree early on Wednesday threatened to retaliate against Red Sea ports in Saudi Arabia if the coalition went ahead with strikes on Hodeida.
“The port of Jeddah, along with all other Saudi enemy ports along the Red Sea coast, will become targets for our forces should the enemy carry out its threats,” he posted on Telegram.
Saree warned civilians near Saudi ports to “evacuate immediately” and called for “all shipping companies to remove their vessels from these ports at once”.
Symbolic strikes

Months into the renewed war, Saudi Arabia appears increasingly unable to shield even its most sensitive infrastructure from attacks, with the Houthis striking strategic facilities across the kingdom and prominent skyscrapers in the heart of Riyadh.

On the ground in Yemen, the Houthis are pressing their advance against government forces, forcing them to retreat. Houthi fighters are positioned just 60 kilometres (37 miles) from Aden, the government’s main stronghold in the south.
A Yemeni military spokesman said this week that they were preparing Aden’s defences for a potential attack.

In a sign of mounting pressure on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia last week removed its top general overseeing its military campaign, in what appeared to be an effort to inject new momentum into the war and contain their adversaries.
On Tuesday, the Saudi capital’s tallest skyscraper was struck for a second time in days, wounding 11 people.
The Houthis claimed responsibility on Wednesday, also saying they struck the sprawling Ras Tanura refinery in the kingdom’s oil-rich east.
Saree described the refinery attack as “accurate and direct”, saying it “caused fires to break out at the facility”.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early Wednesday they had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura, resulting in falling shrapnel but no reported injuries.
Saree said the Houthi attack on Riyadh was carried out in three phases, with strikes also hitting their targets “accurately”.

The Riyadh attack struck the PIF tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund. The building had already been targeted last Thursday and is one of several high-profile sites hit since fighting resumed in the summer.
Attacks on the PIF are symbolic as the fund is driving efforts to diversify the oil-reliant Saudi economy — a project that has been complicated by the Middle East war and Houthi strikes.
Qatar and Pakistan, who have been acting as mediators in efforts to end the wider regional war between Iran and the United States, both “strongly” condemned the attack on the building.

d2f61fe1c22e6831: Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down.

An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley, chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks.

The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again?
For operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving.
One bad node and everybody suffers

On Frontier, a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley says uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up.

Its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide.
Memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck.

In a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened.
Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training.
One failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it.
The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem.
How often should you hit save?

Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch.
The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself.

Vasudevan explains this with an example. If writing a checkpoint takes 30 seconds, saving every five minutes consumes roughly 10 percent of computing time. Stretch that interval to 50 minutes, and the overhead drops to about 1 percent. But a failure could wipe out considerably more work.

Atchley says the calculation depends on the job's size and expected failure rate. He uses an example of ten-hour mean time between failures for a full machine job on Frontier. Using half the machine would roughly double that interval. The Young-Daly checkpointing model helps find the balance between saving too frequently and risking too much work.

Researchers also have the scheduler to contend with. Frontier's standard batch queue limits larger jobs to 12 hours, with shorter limits for smaller jobs. Its extended queue permits jobs of up to 64 nodes to run for 24 hours.
Then there's storage. Checkpoints can be written to the Lustre-based Orion filesystem or node-local SSDs. The faster the data can be saved, the less time checkpointing steals from the actual science.
Restarting is the easy part, but catching up isn't

Before recovery can begin, someone has to notice the job has stalled. Vasudevan says frameworks such as PyTorch can spend several minutes waiting before a hung process is recognized. Operators then have to sift through application logs and hardware telemetry to try to identify the offending GPU.

This can mean another encounter with the scheduler, which decides when replacement resources become available. Once allocated, the application still needs to load its libraries, initialize the runtime, and rebuild communication connections between processors.
And that's before the lost work enters the picture.

Restarting from a checkpoint means returning to the last saved state, potentially hours earlier, and repeating every calculation that has been completed since. The hardware may be back in action, but the simulation hasn't caught up.
Atchley says Frontier can launch a scheduled job in roughly 30 seconds. Restoring the application's data and getting back to useful computation takes longer.
Worse, researchers who lose their allocation may have to rejoin the queue. Depending on demand, Atchley says, "it might take me a day or so before my job runs again."
The machine is up. Where's the science?
Keeping a supercomputer available is one thing. Making sure its processors are doing useful work is another, and the difference is measurable.

A 2026 study by researchers Carlo Graziani, Bethany Lusch, and Bronson Messer examined computational efficiency using records of 331,640 jobs run on Frontier during 2024. Their model estimated that, even with optimally timed checkpoints, only 95.7 percent of allocated computing resources would go toward useful calculations.
The remaining 4.3 percent? Around 1.2 percent goes to writing checkpoints, 2.8 percent disappears into failures, and another 0.3 percent is spent restarting applications.

Skipping checkpoints altogether would be worse. The model puts useful computation at just 91.4 percent without proactive checkpointing, demonstrating that saving work has a cost, but losing it can cost considerably more.

These efficiency figures are modeled estimates, not measurements of every source of lost productivity. They don't capture every delay from rejoining queues, stalled applications, or poorly performing components. The actual productivity bill can be harder to pin down.

This makes Frontier's reported 98.49 percent overall availability in 2024 an interesting contrast. The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's operational assessment measures how often the system was available to users.
Scale makes these losses expensive. An hour of wasted computation across 2,000 nodes represents 2,000 node hours gone, compared with just 100 node hours for a job using 100 nodes.
When the backup needs a backup
Saving checkpoints to local SSDs can speed things up, but there's a catch. If the node fails, the checkpoint stored on it can disappear too.

Atchley points to techniques such as Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR), which can copy checkpoint data to neighboring nodes. This gives applications another recovery point if the original node goes down.

Keeping spare nodes available can also shorten recovery time. Atchley says researchers who reserve extra nodes will consume their computing allocation even if nothing breaks, which leaves fewer hours for useful computation.

Software developers are also trying to avoid the restart process altogether. Vasudevan describes techniques that attempt to transfer distributed application state to replacement hardware to allow synchronized workloads to continue without returning to an earlier checkpoint.

Some approaches can handle certain GPU and network failures through failover. These techniques depend on detecting faults quickly, preserving consistent application state, and having replacement resources available.

None of this makes failures disappear. Atchley notes that hardware improvements, including stronger memory protection, can address problems encountered on earlier machines. But as systems grow, new failure modes emerge.

The next generation of supercomputers may fix the faults that plagued their predecessors, but that doesn't mean they'll never break. Atchley explains that problems solved on one machine tend to give way to entirely new ones on the next.

Faster processors and more memory are only useful if scientists can keep their calculations moving. This makes fault detection and recovery every bit as important as another headline-grabbing performance record.
Resilience research, Atchley admits, "is not sexy at all." But when you're dealing with machines of this size, "scale just amplifies everything." ®

b0deea04c96bb290: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.
Transparency, monetized

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.

The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.
The AI detection problem

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”
Everything’s on the table

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

a9e97e808dea3e7c: A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.
The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its plans for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.
One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

The government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

"The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," said NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

Many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading. Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

Another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

"Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo."
Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.
Current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®
da5d56f9434278b1: WASHINGTON: The Trump administration is poised to imminently release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Tuesday, with new import duties on a wide range of goods expected.
The results of the investigation are expected as soon as Tuesday afternoon, these people said.
The US Trade Representative's (USTR) office is expected to propose new duties that would stack on top of previous tariffs already imposed during president Donald Trump's second term.
The duties would partly replace tariffs struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The administration's tariffs have in part contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the US, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November's midterm elections showed 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs.
Tailored tariff rates

It is unclear what tariff rates would be proposed. One of the people said that the duties would be specifically tailored to each country, with goods from Mexico and Norway unlikely to see any immediate levies.
USTR has been investigating most of the US's largest trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 over what it called evidence of excess industrial capacity.

The White House is expected to honor capped tariff rates that were included in finalised US trade deals with partner countries, this person said. These include duty caps of 15% on goods from the EU, Japan and South Korea and 19% for Malaysia.

The US also is expected to honor the 20% cap on Trump's second-term tariffs on goods from China, as long as a trade truce due to expire on Jan 10 is extended. If it expires, the Chinese excess capacity rate would rise to a higher level.
The US Trade Representative's office and the White House did not respond to Reuters queries about the pending announcement.
Ryan Majerus, a former senior commerce department trade official, said he expects a lengthy report that could include differentiated tariff remedies for each of the 16 trading partners.
Majerus, a partner with King & Spalding, said the administration could propose high tariff rates of 15% to 25% on imports from countries deemed to have excess capacity in various sectors.
Those levies would stack on top of existing tariffs of 10% or 12.5% imposed under a separate investigation into lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws.

However, he said the administration could also propose lower tariff rates with escalation clauses that would ratchet rates higher over time unless countries take steps to reduce excess production capacity.
Replacement tariffs

The trading partners included in the probe are China, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia, along with the EU.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the probe's results could be unveiled as soon as this week.
USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, along with a separate probe into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws in 59 countries and the EU.
Together, the duties are meant to rebuild Trump's global "Liberation Day" tariffs that were struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods.
China has rejected the accusations, saying its exports reflect competitive advantages.
The probe is also partly directed at Chinese investment into countries in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

Under a US-China trade truce due to expire on Jan 10, the Trump administration has capped second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20%, in addition to duties of about 25% imposed during Trump's first term.
The US has already imposed a 12.5% anti-forced labour duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5% to reach the 20% cap.
The US and China are also working to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of non-strategic imports from each side.
afccdcb010158c67: If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home
Originally published on Global Voices
Court of Appeal building in Lagos, Nigeria. Image by King ChristLike via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This post by Fatima Zahra Yahaya is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In February 2025, a letter from a jailed man named Thomas Jonathan Biodun reached the public after some Nigerian Twitter influencers visited his prison to play a friendly football match with the inmates. Biodun was in jail over a debt of NGN 1,137,000 (USD 758). In the letter, he said he had asked for help online before, but someone had called him a scammer.

One of the influencers shared the letter on social media. Another influencer, Sir Dickson, who goes by the handle Wizarab10 on X, pushed it further, garnering over 2.5 million views in one post. In his post, Sir Dickson said, “Nobody should be in prison over a debt. It is not a criminal offense. I have spoken to @egi_nupe [another X influencer and lawyer], and we will be taking it up. Imagine rotting in prison because you’re poor.” A public donation campaign followed, and within weeks, it had raised enough money to clear the debt.
Punch Newspapers reported that Biodun walked out of Apapa Kirikiri Correctional Center and thanked everyone who helped.
Biodun’s story has a happy ending. But it raises a hard question: Should a person’s freedom depend on the benevolence of internet strangers and how many people share a post?
The problem behind this story

In February 2026, the Nigerian Correctional Service said that most people in its custody were still waiting for trial. Many of them have not been found guilty of any crime but remain in pre-trial detention. While some of them cannot pay bail, others cannot pay court fines. In Nigeria, the crime of being poor can land you in a jail cell.

Waiting is not a small thing. While a case drags on, a person may lose their job, business, or place to live. A family can lose its breadwinner, which can derail a whole family — or even a whole community’s livelihoods.
When the internet steps in
Jonathan Biodun is not the only person who turned to the internet to seek support for injustice.

Quadri Alabi, 17, went viral in 2023 when he stood in front of former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi’s campaign convoy. He spent months in Kirikiri Prison over a robbery charge that his lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, called baseless. Effiong also said the police recorded him under the wrong age, meaning he was charged and sentenced as an adult. On April 17, 2025, he was freed. The same day, Effiong asked the public on X to help his family move to a safer home, because they were still getting threats. The International Center for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) reported that more than NGN 3 million (over USD 21,965) was raised within two hours.

Emeka Nzeruike was arrested in 2015, when he was only 12 years old, over an alleged theft. He spent 10 years in prison waiting for trial. In July 2025, a lawyer named Alexander Nzeadi, who posts on X as @_youfoundalex, took up his case, and Emeka walked out of court.

The lawyer wrote that Emeka had been alone, afraid, and forgotten, with no trial and no lawyer. He then asked Nigerians to help Emeka heal, learn a skill, and start his life again now that he was finally free. The post was seen millions of times.
The other side of the story

Look closely at these cases. Biodun, Alabi, and Nzeruike were helped because their stories reached the right people. A letter found the right hands. A lawyer or a kind stranger posted at the right time.
Biodun said he was first called a scammer. That shows how difficult it can be to be believed online.
But what about the person nobody posts about? Not every inmate has a famous friend, a lawyer, or a loud voice to advocate on their behalf. For them, it can feel like no one is watching.
This is the worry. If help comes only to the stories that go viral, then luck decides who goes home. A sad story with a clear photo may win hearts, while a quiet case may be missed.
Raising money to pay for inmates’ legal fees or fines is not new, and it is not only done online.

In 2023, The Conclave reported that public-spirited people and a group called Prisoners Rehabilitation and Welfare Action (PRAWA), a non-governmental organization (NGO), paid fines to free 37 inmates from Kuje and Suleja prisons. The Interior Minister at the time had urged Nigerians to pay the fines of some prisoners to ease crowding in prisons.
Kindness is good. But justice should not depend on luck or others’ generosity.
A hope for smart leaders

I do not believe we should stop being kind. I believe we should fix the courts, so that kindness is not the only hope a poor person has. If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home.
Social media is already doing one useful thing. It shows us real faces and real stories where the system is failing. Smart leaders, lawyers, and judges can listen, and they can fix it.
Until then, every shared post is a sign that Nigerians care. It is also a sign that the courts must do better. Everyone in Nigeria deserves a fair day in court.
Written by Guest Contributor
ca171ab41a233d37: LONDON, Nov 25 — Household energy bills for millions of Britons are set to surge by more than a quarter from January, the sector regulator Ofgem announced today, as the Middle East war drives up wholesale gas prices.
The US-Iran conflict, which sharply reduced tanker traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz, has sent oil and gas prices soaring and raised concerns about a fresh spike in overall inflation.
Ofgem, which sets every quarter the price cap that suppliers can charge customers for electricity and gas, said the cap would increase 26 per cent in January.
That will add around £443 (RM2,385) to the typical annual bill, which will climb to about £2,166, Ofgem said.

“Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches,” said Ofgem’s director general for markets, Neil Kenward.

The increase will impact around 20 million households on standard contracts with variable tariffs. A further 10 million households on fixed-rate deals will be shielded from the rise as long as their contract remains in place.
The price hike means that millions of households will face higher payments even after the government hands out direct subsidies of £100 towards energy bills.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government announced the one-off payment for 20 million households in its annual budget report in October, while also removing fixed fees on gas bills.
The government has also extended a temporary tax cut on household electricity prices.

Since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on 28 February, the price of European natural gas, measured by the Dutch TTF futures contract, has surged by around 190 per cent, rising to €92 per megawatt-hour from around €32.
Britain’s annual inflation rate reached a 12-month high in October at 3.6 per cent as the Middle East conflict drove up motor fuel costs.
The latest energy price cap increase is set to fuel inflation further next year, adding to cost-of-living pressures.
However, gas prices remain well below the levels seen at the height of the energy crisis in 2022 after Russia began its invasion of Ukraine.
The sharpest increase in the price cap came in October 2022, when it was raised by 80 per cent. — AFP
1c069dbd608e2ac1: PETALING JAYA: IOI Properties Group Malaysia Real Estate Investment Trust (IOIPG REIT) fell as much as 5% below its initial public offering (IPO) price of 91 sen on its Main Market debut.

Malaysia’s largest ever REIT IPO raised about RM2 billion for IOI Properties Group Bhd, the sponsor of IOIPG REIT.
The lacklustre debut comes after the trust cut the final IPO price by five sen from the initial indicative retail price of 96 sen, following tepid investor response.
A portion of the IPO was undersubscribed and was reallocated to other categories of investors. The Malaysian public portion of the IPO was oversubscribed by just 0.59 times.

The spin-off listing is part of efforts by IOI Properties to pare down its substantial borrowings and strengthen its balance sheet. It previously stated it was also exploring a separate trust for its Singapore assets.

IOIPG REIT has a portfolio of nine properties valued at RM7.66 billion, anchored by the flagship IOI City Mall in Putrajaya. It also has six hotels operating under Marriott International’s brands and two office developments.
Meanwhile, IOI Properties group CEO and IOIPG REIT executive chairman Lee Yeow Seng defended the pricing of the IPO.
He said the final IPO price of 91 sen per unit matches the trust’s pro forma net asset value (NAV) per unit.

“We don’t want to price the IPO to the maximum, where there’s no upside and nothing left on the table for the investors.
“What we want to try to achieve is to create value for our stakeholders, including our investors, our tenants, as well as our partners,” he added.
Kenanga Investment Bank initiated coverage on IOIPG REIT with an “outperform” call and target price (TP) of RM1.20 while Affin Hwang Investment Bank issued a “buy” call with a TP of RM1.12.

7f46162ddd2d3fe1: A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

This case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision says Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors showed evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”

Another item of evidence apparently showed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”
Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ says.
