3c480a030749f4c3: SINGAPORE: US-listed exchange-traded funds investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent selloff in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.

A net US$4.71 billion has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions this month, also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.

The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto-market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% this month and was trading around US$59,200 as of 1pm Wednesday in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session.

The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up.

Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure.

“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades around the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds at the moment, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following recent US midterm elections. The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode.

“The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.”

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates toward equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.
Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now,” Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning.”
The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said.

“I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why Bitcoin?”

c33bcd47cf0102df: VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues.
VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks:
Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.

The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs.
This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off.
Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

9ee484497e4a362a: DHAKA, Nov 25 — Bangladesh’s garment workers won a 36 per cent minimum wage increase today, officials said, after weeks of sometimes violent protests causing hundreds of millions of dollars in business losses.
The South Asian nation, the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, has seen widespread demonstrations since October by workers demanding higher pay.

The garment industry, which clothes millions of consumers across Europe and North America, is Bangladesh’s economic lifeline, generating four-fifths of export earnings and employing more than four million people.
After the deal was struck following lengthy negotiations with factory owners, workers’ representatives urged people to return to factories.
“Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either,” Babul Akhter, the labour representative on a wage board set up to resolve the crisis, told reporters.
“Previously, workers used to get a wage revision every five years, but this time they are getting a revised wage after three years.”
It was not immediately clear how workers — who clashed with police in industrial zones yesterday — would react to the deal.
Workers initially demanded a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (RM1,000), up from 12,500 taka.
They say their pay has failed to keep pace with the rising cost of food, housing, transport and health care.
Judge Syed Azad Subhani, the chairman of the government-appointed garment industry wage board, said the “majority supported a minimum wage of 17,000 taka”, after a vote early today.
The wage hike will take effect in January.
‘Export engine’

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday that protests had cost the industry an estimated US$428 million in losses, while orders worth US$254 million had shifted to other countries.
The disruption came ahead of the busy Christmas season.
The garment industry, which supplies major international brands including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss, earns around US$38 billion a year.
Bangladesh supplies more than 150 countries with ready-made garments, according to the BGMEA, which represents around 4,000 factories.
The United States is its biggest individual market, while the European Union is its largest trading bloc.
When Bangladesh won independence from Pakistan in 1971, it was among the world’s poorest countries, with its economy devastated by war.
The expansion of garment production helped transform the nation of around 170 million people from a predominantly agricultural economy into a major global manufacturing hub.
Bangladesh’s central bank calls the garment sector the “country’s export engine”.
But its success has been built on a vast, relatively low-paid workforce, with longstanding disputes over wages, working conditions and labour rights.

The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse, which killed more than 1,100 people and injured thousands, exposed appalling safety conditions in the industry, with workers employed in dangerous buildings and often lacking adequate labour protections.

The disaster prompted major international efforts to improve workplace standards, including an agreement between global clothing brands and trade unions to inspect factories and enforce safety measures. — AFP
f38105e96259c3cb: HONG KONG, Nov 25 — Technology firms once again tumbled today as the euphoria that greeted the return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang was washed away by the now-common panic and uncertainty over the AI boom.

News that the poster child of the artificial intelligence explosion had returned less than two weeks after resigning over extramarital affairs — including with an alleged Chinese spy — sent Asian markets into a swoon yesterday.
Traders were reassured about the ongoing presence of a fixer and visionary to an industry that has fuelled a tech revolution and a global economic boom.

But the mood appeared to have already soured as analysts pointed to the reality that there were still huge worries about the colossal sums pumped into the AI buildout and when they would see returns, if any.
After explosive gains yesterday, Asian stock markets were back in the doldrums.
Taipei, Tokyo and Seoul — home of most of the region’s key AI-linked firms — sank 8 per cent, more than 3 per cent and more than 5 per cent, respectively.
That came a day after surging 9 per cent, 3.9 per cent and more than 6 per cent respectively.
The losses were led by Taiwan’s TSMC and MediaTek, Japanese chip giants Kioxia and Advantest, and South Korean titans SK hynix and Samsung.
There was also heavy selling in Shanghai, Sydney and Singapore. However, Hong Kong, Wellington and Manila edged up.

The rout followed a return to reality on Wall Street, where Nvidia — which had rocketed more than 31 per cent Monday — shed almost 6 per cent, while AI giant Anthropic lost 6.5 per cent to fall below last week’s US$83 (RM341.30) IPO price.
AMD, Intel and Micron also took a hammering after the previous day’s surge.
The Nasdaq shed 1.5 per cent and the S&P 500 lost 0.5 per cent but the Dow rose, with analysts pointing out that traders were rotating into other sectors.
‘Dead-cat bounce’
“The champagne from (the) Nvidia resurrection had barely lost its fizz before Wall Street was back reaching for the sick bags,” said SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“What looked like the mother of all relief rallies has already acquired the rather less flattering characteristics of a dead-cat bounce, with the Nasdaq taking another beating (and) Nvidia surrendering a sizeable chunk of its extraordinary gains.
He said “professional investors (were) apparently using the opening provided by the Jensen Huang comeback to unload technology exposure rather than rebuild it”.
“And that, unfortunately, is what happens when a market rallies on the back of forced buying rather than genuine conviction.”

And BNZ’s Jason Wong added: “Despite Huang’s return, some key issues continue to overhang the AI sector, including whether investment in the sector will provide an adequate return and the threat of regulation under a new administration from next year.”
Nvidia also remains under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to the firm’s top-line chips.
Investors will be keeping an eye on the release of the Federal Reserve’s preferred gauge of inflation later in the day, which could play a role in its interest rate decision next month.
With price gains still far above target, officials are widely expected to hike, but their post-meeting statement will be pored over for an idea about the bank’s plans for the new year.

In company news, Chinese electronics giant Xiaomi jumped 8 per cent in Hong Kong on optimism for the performance of the company’s higher-end smartphones even as an AI-driven memory chip supply crunch hits profits. — AFP
3e6bca11ce95d356: Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.
Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.”

Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO said the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”

News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix announced its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®

aa33fe05c91dcee3: Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”

The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”
HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company.
Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”
“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”

HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

Dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®

ec7b63860efa33d3: Malaysia Athletics cannot claim to have put its house in order while Karim Ibrahim remains president of one of its affiliates despite his disqualification by World Athletics.
Karim is not only the former president of Malaysia Athletics. He also heads Perak Athletics Association (Perak AA), a member of the national body.
MA’s endorsed constitution appears clear on the eligibility of people in such positions.

Article 13.2.8 bars anyone disqualified, removed or suspended by MA, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority from being nominated, elected, appointed or holding office as an affiliate’s office-bearer, council member or committee member.
That restriction remains until the relevant authority lifts the sanction or the person succeeds in an appeal.

World Athletics has disqualified Karim. He has not appealed, and the sanction remains in force. The provision expressly covers office-holders in MA’s affiliates, not just those serving on its national executive council.

His position in Perak AA therefore puts MA’s responsibility to enforce its own constitution squarely in focus. The national body cannot leave the state association to decide whether it wishes to observe a rule that binds its members.
Affiliation carries obligations
MA’s authority to demand compliance rests on more than the eligibility provision.

Article 18.3 gives its constitution and by-laws precedence when they conflict with those of its members. Article 18.4 requires MA, its affiliates and people holding positions under its rules to comply with Malaysian law and the regulations of OCM, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics and other relevant international sports bodies.
Together, these clauses establish the obligations that come with membership. A state association cannot claim the benefits of affiliation while disregarding the rules governing the sport.
There is, however, a difference between requiring an affiliate to comply with MA’s constitution and automatically rewriting its registered rules.
If Perak AA’s constitution conflicts with the national one, it may still have to follow its own amendment procedures and the requirements of Malaysian law.

That does not excuse inaction. MA should formally notify Perak AA of the eligibility provision, explain its application and require the state body to address the position of its office-holders in accordance with the rules.

The same scrutiny should extend to every affiliate. MA must identify conflicting provisions or practices in state associations and set out what they need to do to comply. It should not wait for another dispute to expose weaknesses in its governance.
The council must be prepared to act
The executive council has a clear role in this process.

Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret MA’s constitution and by-laws. Article 16.2 provides a mechanism for disputes between MA and its members, or between members. The council may seek OCM’s advice before making its final decision by majority.
These provisions give the council a way to resolve disagreements. They also place responsibility on it to address non-compliance.

That does not give the council licence to impose whatever penalty it chooses. It must identify the relevant breach, follow the proper procedures and give the affiliate a fair opportunity to respond. Any action must also comply with Malaysian law.
But procedural requirements should guide enforcement, not become an excuse to avoid it.

In Perak AA’s case, the council should establish the facts, determine the application of Article 13.2.8 and set out the steps needed to bring the state body into compliance. If Perak AA disputes the interpretation, the constitution provides a route to resolve the matter.

The same standards must apply to every affiliate. Perak AA should not receive special treatment because Karim once led the national association. Nor should any state body enjoy an exemption because of its influence or leadership.

This is not about stripping state associations of their autonomy. They should remain free to run their programmes, develop athletes and manage their affairs. But autonomy does not mean freedom to disregard the rules of the national and international sport.
The Karim episode exposed the consequences of a national body allowing its own rules to fall short of international requirements. MA must not allow that failure to continue at state level.
Its constitution gives it the authority to demand compliance. The executive council must now show that it has the resolve to use it.

3fa3cdca329aa8c5: Ironi adalah perkataan yang sepatutnya sinonim dengan politik. Apa tidaknya, musuh boleh jadi kawan, kawan boleh jadi musuh, orang yang ditentang reformasi dia pula yang memenangkannya.

Dulu tahun 80-an dan 90-an, saya menyokong Dr Mahathir Mohamad 100%. Kemudian saya amat membenci beliau dari tahun 1997 hingga 2016, berlatarkan reformasi ketika itu. Apabila beliau bekerjasama dengan Pakatan Harapan, saya menyokong Mahathir sehinggalah 2020 apabila beliau ditikam belakang oleh parti sendiri -- sedap juga melihat Mahathir ditikam oleh gengnya sendiri. Sekarang saya menulis pula bahawa pandangan beliau tentang PAS jelas lebih benar berbanding tanggapan saya terhadap parti itu, sejak dari 1997 hingga PAS berkawan dengan Umno dan Najib Razak.

Tujuan saya menulis artikel ini adalah kerisauan saya tentang nilai dan sikap orang Melayu. PAS kini memperlihatkan nilai yang cukup membimbangkan tetapi yang peliknya tak ramai agamawan akademik yang menegur secara langsung. Maka terpaksalah saya mencari orang yang orang Melayu hormat lebih daripada orang kerdil dalam politik seperti saya untuk memberi kesedaran tentang bahaya parti yang menunggang agama demi kuasa.

Baru-baru ini kita membaca tentang seorang pemimpin PAS yang mengatakan pemberian derma untuk membayar denda RM50 juta yang dikenakan ke atas seseorang yang didapati bersalah dalam kes penyelewengan dana adalah perbuatan yang dapat pahala. Sebelum ini, rasanya tahun lepas, PAS menjayakan tabung jihad untuk membayar saman fitnah untuk seorang wakil rakyatnya. Kedua-dua kes penyelewengan dana dan fitnah ini boleh kita telusur tanpa was-was. Kemudian, kita dapat tahu bahawa orang yang memfitnah serta orang yang pecah amanah dan salah guna kedudukan tidak menyatakan penyesalan, jauh lagi berikrar tidak akan mengulang lagi perbuatan.

Tidak cukup dengan itu, kita juga mendengar PAS menggunakan istilah munafik semasa membahaskan Belanjawan 2027 yang dibentangkan perdana menteri baru-baru ini. Ada pula presiden PAS menyifatkan Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan yang ditandatangani antara kerajaan dan beberapa Ahli Parlimen pembangkang sebagai pendekatan dajal. Kita sudah pun maklum tentang peristiwa membaca doa qunut nazilah terhadap orang yang tidak sehaluan dengan PAS. Isu mengkafirkan orang sudah pun tercatat dalam sejarah negara.
Maka itu saya menyingkap dua ucapan Mahathir dalam Perhimpunan Agung Umno pada 1984 dan 1999. Dalam ucapan 1984, Mahathir mengecam PAS seperti berikut;

"Umno adalah parti politik orang Melayu. Oleh kerana orang Melayu semuanya beragama Islam, maka Umno dengan sendirinya menjadi parti orang Islam Semenanjung Malaysia dan berjuang untuk agama Islam. Tetapi Umno bukan hipokrit dan berpura-pura menafikan yang ia adalah parti orang Melayu seperti yang dibuat oleh sebuah parti lain.

"Umno dengan jelas mengakui yang ianya parti kebangsaan Melayu di samping menjadi parti Islam. Menafi hakikat ini akan menjadikannya hipokrit atau munafik -- dan orang munafik tidak menjadi orang Islam yang jujur.

"Tidak ada cara yang lebih berkesan untuk mengekalkan kelemahan orang Melayu daripada menggunakan orang Melayu sendiri untuk melawan orang Melayu. Dengan tertubuhnya PAS maka terbentuklah alat utama musuh orang Melayu. Malang bagi mereka, kebanyakan daripada orang Melayu dapat meneka strategi pecah-belah ini dan telah terus menyokong Umno.

"Sekarang ini usaha ditumpukan kepada melemahkan semangat kebangsaan Melayu dengan mendakwa Islam menentang kebangsaan. Bahawa kebangsaan orang Melayu adalah satu alat mempertahankan diri bagi orang Melayu yang semuanya Islam, sama seperti kebangsaan Mujahidin mempertahankan orang Islam Afghanistan, dan tidak menjadi satu keangkuhan yang mengenepikan agama Islam dan orang Islam lain, tidak disebut. Mereka yang mendakwa bahawa mereka cuma mengakui keislaman mereka dan kononnya menolak semangat kebangsaan Melayu, tidak pula berani mempertahankan orang yang seagama dengan mereka di Afghanistan, atau di Lubnan atau di lain-lain tempat. Keislaman mereka terhad kepada kegiatan di Malaysia sahaja di mana kebangsaan Melayu Umno dapat memberi perlindungan kepada mereka. Sifat mereka ini adalah sifat hipokrit atau sifat talam dua muka. Dan mereka adalah begitu fanatik kepada parti mereka sehingga mereka tidak menyoal sama ada pendirian parti mereka baik atau tidak. Mereka inilah yang sebenarnya dari golongan asabiyah."
Jelas siapa sebenarnya hipokrit yang dimaksudkan Mahathir ketika itu. Namun demikian kita dapat merasai kesamaan mesej tersebut dalam tindak tanduk PAS ketika ini.

Dalam petikan kedua ucapan yang sama, Mahathir mempertikaikan PAS bahawa mereka sahaja yang tahu Islam manakala orang lain seperti Umno ketika itu yang juga mempunyai barisan pemimpin seperti Anwar Ibrahim tidak mencerminkan Islam sebenar.

"Sebagai satu lagi usaha untuk menentukan kejayaan orang Melayu, kita telah berusaha menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam. Kita tidak syak bahawa nilai-nilai Islam akan menjadikan orang Melayu orang yang lebih berjaya di dunia dan di akhirat. Pentadbiran yang diasaskan kepada nilai-nilai Islam tetap akan menjadi pentadbiran yang kukuh, adil dan berjaya.

"Di sini nilai-nilai Islam tidak bermakna rupa bentuk dan kebudayaan Arab yang menjadi tumpuan setengah-setengah orang Melayu di Malaysia. Memang benar rupa-bentuk boleh dijadikan simbol Islam dan ditiru dengan mudah. Tetapi rupa-bentuk tidak akan membawa kejayaan kepada kita. Yang akan membawa kejayaan ialah amalan nilai-nilai Islam seperti amanah, disiplin, taat setia, rajin dan tekun, bersaudara antara orang-orang mukmin, berani kerana benar, bertoleransi dan bertimbang rasa, adil, insaf dan syukur dan lain-lain lagi nilai yang mulia yang tidak begitu mudah diamal atau dipamerkan.

"Dalam ucapan saya di perhimpunan agung 1982, saya telah menjelaskan tentang hasrat kerajaan untuk menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam ke dalam pentadbiran negara. Maksud saya ialah supaya kita akan mentadbir dengan amanah, jujur, disiplin, setia, bertanggungjawab, cekap, bersih, dan lain-lain lagi nilai Islam yang akan menjadikan pentadbiran negara ini satu pentadbiran yang berkesan dan adil.

"Malangnya hasrat ini telah dijadikan alasan untuk ajaran dan tindakan yang membawa masalah dan mengganggu pentadbiran. Islam sengaja digambarkan oleh kumpulan-kumpulan tertentu sebagai agama yang tidak toleran, sehingga kakitangan kerajaan yang beragama Islam dilarang dari berkawan dengan yang bukan Islam dan melawat mereka di hari kebesaran mereka. Tumpuan diberikan bukan kepada soal khidmat yang baik dan pegangan kepada janji dan ikrar, tetapi kepada soal haram-halal, di mana tafsiran dibuat mengikut nafsu.

"Demikianlah ekstremnya tafsiran yang dibuat sehingga ada pegawai yang tidak mahu menyentuh kertas yang ada tertulis di dalamnya perkataan 'babi'. Ada yang sanggup menukar arahan ketua kerana tidak secocok dengan fahaman ekstrim mereka. Ada yang berpendapat bahawa penerapan nilai Islam bermakna memakai cador, tetapi kerana gaji, mereka masih sanggup bekerja di pejabat."

Dalam petikan ucapan 1999 sewaktu era reformasi dan Mahathir berseteru dengan Anwar, beliau juga menyerang PAS yang bekerjasama dengan DAP. Di sini Mahathir menyebut bahawa PAS adalah parti yang boleh mengubah haluan mengikut citarasa sendiri dan memfatwakan apa saja bagi niat politik kuasa;

"PAS adalah sebuah parti yang mudah menukar haluan mengikut kepentingan semasa. Demikian pada mulanya PAS mendakwa bahawa orang Islam yang bekerjasama dengan orang bukan Islam menjadi kafir dan dengan itu PAS menolak kerjasama dengan bukan Islam. Kemudian PAS menyertai Barisan Nasional dan bekerjasama dengan orang bukan Islam dalam BN. Pada masa itu PAS tidak lagi mendakwa bahawa orang Islam yang bekerjasama dengan bukan Islam menjadi kafir. Ternampak jelas tafsiran agama oleh PAS boleh ditukar untuk kepentingan semasa.

"Kemudian PAS keluar daripada BN dan menganggap orang Umno tidak Islam sehingga ahli dan pemimpin PAS sanggup sembahyang berasingan di masjid yang sama dan membina masjid lain bagi orang PAS. Tetapi apabila pilihan raya hampir tiba, PAS mengadakan pakatan dengan DAP yang bukan Islam. Bagi PAS, orang Umno yang Islam tidak boleh dijadikan sahabat seperti PAS bersahabat dengan orang bukan Islam dalam DAP."
Kini kita melihat kebenaran kata-kata Mahathir itu apabila PAS menghumban Bersatu dan memeluk Umno serta kini memperjuangkan nasib Najib.
Akhir sekali Mahathir menyinggung isu PAS yang suka merendahkan umat Islam lain dan menampakkan diri mereka seperti orang Islam terpilih dan special dalam ungkapan seperti di bawah;

"Hari ini kita lihat kesan daripada kesanggupan PAS bekerjasama dengan syaitan. Nik Aziz dan pemimpin PAS yang lain sanggup mengeluarkan kata-kata yang buruk kononnya Badawi Malaysia menjadi gembala babi. Sindiran ini tidak mempunyai asas kerana Abdullah Badawi telah ditugaskan untuk menyelaraskan kerja-kerja menghapuskan penyakit JE (Japanese Encephalitis), bukan untuk menjaga babi. Lebih dari itu dakwaan dibuat kononnya tuhan mencarut dan kita orang Islam patut mencarut.

"Tetapi orang PAS akan terus setia kepada PAS kerana mereka fanatik dan taasub kepada parti mereka. Mereka adalah daripada kumpulan asabiyah, kumpulan yang terlalu fanatik dalam menyokong kumpulan mereka sehingga tidak mengambilkira kumpulan mereka baik atau jahat, benar atau salah. Demikian apabila ahli PAS berkhalwat, mereka tidak bersalah. Kesalahan hanya ada pada orang lain, tidak sama sekali kepada orang PAS dan parti PAS. Inilah orang yang keterlaluan dan termasuk dalam golongan asabiyah."

Mahathir cukup benar bacaannya tentang PAS serta ahli-ahli yang mempunyai sentimen kefanatikan yang cukup besar. Sikap ini bukan sahaja ada pada golongan tidak berpendidikan tinggi, golongan kelas pertengahan dan akademik berjawatan tinggi di universiti pun sama saja kefanatikan mereka.

Saya menyokong PAS selama 20 tahun, sebagai ahli dan penyumbang wang serta pemikiran. Saya juga membenci semua tuduhan Mahathir terhadap PAS dahulu, tetapi hari ini saya terpaksa mengakui bahawa bacaan Mahathir tentang PAS ternyata benar dan saya dapat melihat dengan sendiri kebenaran tersebut hari ini.

Sebagai ringkasan ucapan Mahathir di atas, beliau membawa mesej tentang bahaya kepercayaan fanatik kepada agama dan parti politik yang boleh merosakkan orang Melayu dan pembinaan negara bangsa serta pembangunan ekonomi untuk semua.

b879995cf1e26209: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

efcebe1c40df74e1: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.
In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.”

“Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed.
“He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.”

LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models.
Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models.

Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year.
The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse.

“Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read.
Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post.

Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his company has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models.
In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own.
LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory.
Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [PDF] in support of open-weights models.

Open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.”

As we previously reported, Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the big model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not.

Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.
The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT.
The Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®
1479a2d5f1158c80: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness. A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles. But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls. “TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.” The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.  The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live. Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month. Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture. The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing. Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious. “The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.” A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life. Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.
e41a71b86838ecc4: Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño. AP Photo/Charlie RiedelThe extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars. This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models. Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. El Nino’s effects, especially strong in 2026, have disrupted crops and supply chains around the world, including a delayed monsoon season in India. Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images What this means for supply chains The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models. When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services. While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin. What it means for consumers Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year. And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026. A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth. Suvrat Dhanorkar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

1e5a5d482e355f68: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.

That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.

As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of "dry hopping" (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.

fdd5f51e8fafafb3: Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal's total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it's only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.

5757249a1e5ac515: It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.
22995c289ab600a9: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide. The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights. Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya. The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya. Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility. The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army. The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state. The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided. But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law. Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it. The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs. How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs. Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance. Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps. More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026. Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed. It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community. Not ‘illegal immigrants’ Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine. The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice. San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
e2ba0e13f0a1a55f: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families. “I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change. For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom. For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English. Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue. A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues. Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population. I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities. In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali. For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue. Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk. Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues. In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support. In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.” Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID), CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams. Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale. In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.” Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.” Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained. Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education. Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them. From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.” Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities. Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues. Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they. Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

89de79cca67002c9: DENIS ESAULOV 1987/ShutterstockThe recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems. It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda. Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers. Ending unanimity Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap. In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting). Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters. So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions. A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets. The Cop climate negotiation process hinges on all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. metamorworks/Shutterstock It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend). It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration (issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business. Coalition of the willing Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?” This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks. Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results. As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute. The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero). We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats. Francesco Grillo is Director of the think tank Vision.

Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You’ll Be the Main Character

Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.

Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The and parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”

It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says.

The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”

The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+.

The people generating AI slop on social media are making incredibly specific content because they know that social media algorithms will be highly effective at filtering people there. Meta is already allowing advertisers to use AI to generate many slightly different versions of an advertisement; its targeting AI then automatically shows them to users who are most likely to react to a specific version of an ad. As I’ve previously reported, TCL has been experimenting with AI-generated content on its streaming free TV channels, and, even without AI-generated content, free streaming TV channels have gotten incredibly specific. It is now possible, for example, to watch reruns of individual shows 24/7/365.

AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea.

As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that alters spoken words (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.
