f82e2058d3bb9c30: Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.  Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way. Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages. “Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper. The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing. Parsing the linguistic mind Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere. “Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center. While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way. For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker? It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence. Where AI meets the brain Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing lens into the human mind. Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope. “Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach. Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input. Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages. A mental bridge between languages The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages. “We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.” Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication. What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko. In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out. In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko. De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.
1e8d527100dd7796: On Nov. 22, the day after COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya, Turkey, the global average temperature at noon UTC was estimated to be a record-setting 2.36 C above the pre-industrial average. Climate change is driving up global temperatures. Yet governments could not even agree to name the fossil fuels driving it. I have been a climate scientist since the late 1980s and have followed every UN climate summit since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. I cannot recall a more embarrassing failure than COP31. The first draft proposed at least US$120 billion by 2035 to help countries adapt to climate change. By Nov. 19, the figure was gone. Three years ago in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. The Nov. 16 Antalya draft said so plainly. Yet, the final proposal at COP31 still omitted any mention of fossil fuels. The European Union and small island states were right to reject it. Given the recent failure, is it time for scientists and activists to boycott COP? From early success to utter failure While COP31 collapsed without an agreement, previous UN climate talks have had successes. In the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, industrialized countries agreed to reduce their collective emissions, averaged over 2008–12, to 5.2 per cent below 1990 levels. Emissions over the 2008-12 reporting period came in 9.9 per cent below 1990 levels. In Paris in 2015, governments agreed to hold warming “well below 2 C above pre-industrial levels” while “pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels.” Yet, in June 2026, a UN report found that the world is set to exceed the 1.5 C global warming target outlined in Paris. In 2015, governments invited the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to report back in 2018 on the impacts of 1.5 C of warming and the emissions pathways that could get us there. In future emissions pathways leading to little or no overshoot of the 1.5 C target, global net carbon dioxide emissions were required to fall roughly 45 per cent from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050. Those pathways also required removing 100 to 1,000 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere over the century (so-called negative emissions) using technology that had yet to be developed. The authors spelled out the difficulties. The key government takeaway was that meeting the 1.5 C target could still be achieved. What struck me was how little those models resembled the world in which people make decisions. You can write carbon removal into a model. Somebody still has to find the land, build the equipment and pay to operate it. You don’t build a coal plant today to tear it down tomorrow. The utility has debt to repay and communities need power. What if we stayed home? Andrew Weaver on BBC News discussing COP31. Scientists, environmentalists and youth groups should boycott the next COP. I further think scientists should also consider walking away from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessments. I was a lead author on four of them. I know what that invitation means to a young scientist, yet at some point, the scientific community needs to speak out as a collective. And those of us who have already had the privilege of working on IPCC assessments ought to speak first — and loudest. The Paris Agreement showed how readily governments can use our willingness to buy time. Ministers agreed on a temperature, asked us what it would mean if the world exceeded it, then continued exploiting fossil fuels regardless. Climate change has become a global tragedy of the commons. Fossil-fuel producers earn money selling their products while sharing the climatic cost with everyone else. Countries and tech companies are incentivized to race ahead with artificial intelligence, regardless of the environmental risks the rest of us inherit. And in our politics, climate change has become subsumed into a culture war where politics rail against green policies regardless of the facts. While Canada’s delegates were in Antalya, Ottawa committed $200 million to expand planned production at Woodfibre LNG, a liquefied natural gas export terminal in British Columbia. With decisions like that, the world is on course to even exceed 2 C of global warming. So, let governments go to the next COP and explain the empty seats. Save the airfare, the emissions and two weeks of time better spent elsewhere. Instead, use a fraction of that time to ask your representatives about the tangible action they are taking to tackle climate change. Andrew Weaver receives funding from NSERC and NRCan. He has previously served as an MLA and leader of the BC Green Party.
c642a9ca0e226b9c: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a U of M blog post.
<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.

“It is widely promoted as the next step in furthering novel research taking place at this University. What is conveniently left out on flyers and pamphlets is that this is only part of the proposition, 10% in fact, the other 90% is being used by Los Alamos — a nuclear weapons developer,” a sophomore studying biochemistry told the board before the vote. “We already have three existing high tech data centers used for research. Why must we push forward with another one that is promoting nuclear warfare?”

An electrician from Ypsilanti Township, a representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) union, supported the construction project. “This will create 300 plus jobs for our members, all local, [and] give back to the community,” he said. “IBEW is in favor of the data center, excuse me, ‘high compute research center.’”

People who attended the regent’s meeting to discuss other topics referenced the vote during their presentations. “You voted today to fund a $785 million data center project in Ypsilanti, much to the opposition of the residents of the area, acting against what many residents in the area are calling environmental racism. I think I can speak for many students when I say I am frankly appalled by this decision,” a student who was there to discuss carbon emissions said.

A library worker present to talk about how the University treats its workers invoked the data center. “I’m not sure I can confidently appeal to your sense of compassion around this. The officials and residents of Ypsi Township are saying ‘stop,’ saying ‘no,’ saying ‘this hurts.’ And you and others responsible for this nuclear weapons data center project have shown you don’t care about the basic issue of consent as you plow ahead,” he said.
Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.

Despite the opposition in the room, the regents approved the project. “It’s been very controversial [...] For me, this is all about an investment in the community and it’s an investment, in many different ways,” regent Denise Ilitch said just before the vote. “The community will be enhanced — they may not feel it now, some, but I venture to say that there will be much good that will come from this.”

Many in Ypsilanti Township disagree. After the regents voted, the leadership and residents of the Township gathered for a panel discussion about the data center. One of the speakers that night was Jay Coghlan, the executive director of Nuclear Watch of New Mexico, a watchdog group that tracks Los Alamos. “The data center issue here in Ypsilanti is unique in that it is the clearest example of the pending merger of AI and nuclear weapons, which doesn’t bode well,” Coghlan told 404 Media.

Coghlan told 404 Media that he shared the Township’s concerns about how the data center will use water and electricity but said he thinks its construction will have farther reaching consequences. “Our nation is transforming from the military-industrial complex that Eisenhower warned us about to a Silicon Valley-Pentagon-Wall Street complex that closely links economics, economic inequality, increasing militarism, and I dare say the rise of techno-fascism,” he said.

U of M has repeatedly said the data center will mostly be used to power medical breakthroughs and conduct cancer research, something it’s highlighted in flyers and pamphlets it’s mailed to people in the Township. LANL sent a letter to the people of the community in September that promised it wouldn't build nuclear weapons in their backyard.

“I'm going ‘Duh, yeah, you're not going to bring plutonium to Ypsilanti in Michigan,” Coghlan said. “But I expect this data center to have a lot to do with the design of new nuclear weapons. So, in that way, Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.”

Coghlan said he finds hope in the opposition to the project. “I’m very impressed by the intensity of opposition that I have witnessed. There seems to be a pretty widespread public awareness of the data center in Ypsilanti, Township.”

During the Township meeting on November 19, after the regents voted, Ypsilanti Township attorney Douglas Winters said he was mad. “What did we learn on November 3rd? Two weeks ago and two days, voters around this country loudly declared that they were sick and tired of government corruption. They were tired of secrecy. They were tired of abuse of power. They were tired of threats to democracy and the disregard of governmental accountability. And, importantly, they also said they were sick and tired of these data centers,” he said. “Somehow that message did not make it to Ann Arbor. That message did not make it to the board of regents.”

Winters and other leaders vowed to keep fighting the data center’s construction. In May, the community’s water authority voted to restrict new construction on infrastructure to data center projects while it conducts a review of their impact on the Township’s water supply. The University called the move “unlawfully discriminatory.” In August, the Township passed a six month moratorium on new electrical infrastructure, a move aimed at delaying the project.
9cbcfc27624697ca: In a 2019 referendum, close to 98% of Bougainvilleans for independence. After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process. In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result. A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving. Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track. The legacy of colonialism Bougainville was named by French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville in the 18th century, and colonialism has shaped its history ever since. In 1899, it was incorporated into German New Guinea, while the neighbouring Solomon Islands became a British protectorate. Colonial control shifted to Australian occupation in 1914, a move legitimised by the League of Nations in 1920. During the second world war, Japanese forces took over, followed by an American-led invasion in 1943. From 1949, Bougainville was again under Australian control as part of PNG. The dismantling of colonial rule began in 1971, and PNG gained independence in 1975. Bougainville’s decolonisation was left unresolved. The crisis years From 1988 to 1998, Bougainville experienced one of the most severe conflicts in the South Pacific. The Panguna mine was a focal point for grievances related to land ownership, environmental damage, a desire for self-determination and the distribution of mining resources. The mine began operating in 1972 in Central Bougainville, and was once one of the world’s one of the world’s largest copper and gold mines. Owned by a subsidiary of the Australian company Rio Tinto, it was a significant source of revenue for the PNG government. In the late 1980s, the environmental impacts of mining and unequal distribution of its revenues led to violent protests by landowners and the closure of the mine. The PNG government responded with force, and the protests developed into an armed rebellion. Conflict ensued, involving the Bougainville Revolutionary Army, the PNG Defence Force and various local factions. Australia provided indirect military support to PNG forces. A years-long PNG-imposed blockade paralysed Bougainville’s government services and economic activity. An estimated 15,000–20,000 lives were lost in the conflict overall. Attempts to end the fighting began with people from local villages, especially women. They used customary and introduced conflict resolution processes, alongside Christian faith, to lay the groundwork for political negotiations. Eventually, peace talks began in 1998, and an agreement was signed in 2001. Two narratives about how peace was achieved There have long been two narratives about Bougainville’s path to peace. One emphasises regional and international diplomacy, which has involved New Zealand‑facilitated talks in 1997–98, unarmed Australian peace monitoring and UN engagement. The second, backed by many Bougainvillean and PNG leaders, stresses a “light intervention” of international support and notes the distinctly Melanesian approach to peacemaking. This process has been inclusive (involving women’s groups, young people, ex-combatants, faith-based organisations and churches) and patient. The Bougainville Peace Agreement In 2001, the Bougainville Peace Agreement established a framework for Bougainville’s political future. The agreement led to the establishment of the autonomous Bougainville government, a weapons-disposal program, free and fair elections, and a referendum on Bougainville’s future political status. The 2019 referendum gave Bougainvilleans a decisive mandate. Then in August of this year, the autonomous Bougainville government and PNG government – with international support – set out a jointly agreed, phased pathway to translate the referendum result into a constitutional transition. Now, the results must be ratified by PNG’s parliament – the final legislative step in the peace agreement process. A “yes” vote will not itself create independence. It will kick off the legal, administrative and institutional actions needed to move towards self‑government and ultimately independence. A “no” or deferred vote will trigger further consultations and protective measures. Panguna, resources and public understanding Even in PNG, not everyone understands the history of the conflict and the nature of the peace process – especially younger people, including parliamentarians. Some have complained Bougainville’s independence would threaten national unity and set a precedent for other provinces. Complex post-conflict issues remain in Bougainville, including unresolved trauma from the years of conflict. This has exacerbated other forms of violence based on gender and accusations of sorcery. Natural resource governance, especially the future of the still-inactive Panguna mine, also remains uncertain. Local communities have led a process that has just seen Rio Tinto agree to pay US$250 million (A$376 million) to begin addressing the long-term environmental and human cost of the mine. Efforts are also being made to diversify an independent Bougainville’s revenue through fishing, farming and the sustainable approach set out in its “green‑blue economy policy”. For many people, Panguna is both an emblem of past dispossession and a potential source of revenue for an independent Bougainville. For others, its reopening would risk reviving conflict. Across the Pacific, community-led peacebuilding efforts aim to prevent conflict alongside providing environmental resilience. While international security pacts are proliferating, practical security on the ground may depend more on addressing colonial legacies, inequality and the impacts of climate change. A way forward Whatever the outcome of the parliamentary vote, the institutions, relationships and habits of joint work built through the peace process give reason for cautious optimism. The people of Bougainville and Papua New Guinea have done the slow work to get to this point. Those of us watching from outside can take this moment to honour the peace process so far and do what is needed to support its future. Tania Miletic was Project Leader of the Bougainville Senior Leadership Professional Development Program 2023-24, an Australian government program, delivered by the University of Melbourne with financial support from the NZ Government.
da45b84cc5fd1d8d: President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesThe story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump, who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks. Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct. It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.” This article was updated on Nov. 23, 2026, to reflect Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. Michael Nalick does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
1ee9f5994a817a2b: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

362b561c4f5d2c55: The farmer-poet Wendell Berry once described a dystopian world where society is singularly directed toward “the objective” – a relentless drive for industrial extraction that leads to the destruction of nature and communities. The idea captured Berry’s concerns about the industrialization of agriculture and the expansion of natural resource extraction that became prominent across rural America in the latter decades of the 20th century. Over nine decades, Berry watched how agribusinesses’ and farm owners’ pursuit of productive efficiency and maximum profits led to machines and synthetic chemicals replacing human farm labor, and the replacement of diversified farms with monocropping and concentrated animal-feeding operations. Across the U.S., he saw small farms disappear, often consolidated into vast corporate businesses with absent owners. What gets lost in this pursuit of production and profit, he noted, are community, human dignity and flourishing, natural beauty and ecological well-being. People are the heart of rural towns, like Waubeka, Wis. Farm consolidation has shrunk many of America’s rural towns since the mid 1900s. AP Photo/Teresa Crawford As agriculture researchers and rural sociologists, we, like Berry, have seen how the industrialization of agriculture has changed the face of rural America and hollowed out its communities. Once-thriving main streets in rural towns have slowly lost their businesses, with fewer farm-related jobs to keep local residents in the area. Machine dealers and suppliers of farm input such as seeds, fertilizer and pesticides have disappeared. Local grocery stores have been replaced by gas station convenience stores. Schools have shrunk or consolidated with the population decline. Hospitals have closed. This “unsettling of America,” in Berry’s words, shows that the farm economy and the rural economy no longer rise and fall together. Rural communities continue to decline despite farm booms and busts. Losing farming’s rural economy multiplier effect Since the late 1940s, the number of farmers in the U.S. has plummeted by nearly 90%, falling from 5.9 million in 1948 to only 715,000 by 2025. During the same period, the agricultural workforce has shifted from mostly farm owners – about 78% – with a few hired hands in 1948 to one today where most of the work is done by farm laborers, about 68% of the workforce. This means profits from farming mainly flow to a small number of farm owners, while the people doing the farm work are paid much less. The loss of small, owner-operated farms, where a farm family could make a living, is one reason many rural communities have lost population over the past century. In prior eras, farming energized rural communities as money circulated in the rural economy, supporting rural businesses and populations – what is termed a “multiplier effect.” Today, local suppliers and services are harder to find, and farm profits instead flow to owners outside the community. Agriculture today resembles capital-intensive natural resource extraction, like mining, where a small number of very profitable businesses operate most acres in the county. Such farms employ few people at low wages, and profits accrue to distant landlords and investment firms. This shift further reinforces rural decline. The farm economy of the 21st century does little to create additional jobs in rural America. An analysis of 11 counties in Iowa found that every US$1 million of agricultural sales creates 2.4 total farm jobs and 1.6 spin-off jobs in other nonfarm businesses, for a total of four new jobs. By contrast, healthcare creates 10 new jobs and construction creates seven new jobs in all for every $1 million in sales. Both pay good wages, which keeps rural people from leaving and helps rural economies thrive. Both also create more spin-off jobs. In short, agriculture produces profits for the company, whereas healthcare and construction produce good-paying jobs for rural residents. More small farms can help communities thrive In the mid-1940s, the U.S. Senate commissioned two studies on the social impacts of economic concentration and corporate monopolies. In one, Walter Goldschmidt, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, described two agricultural communities in California, one with a few large farms and the other with numerous smaller farms. He evaluated the social qualities of each and found that the community with more small farms had a higher standard of living and quality of life than the community with a few large farms. The other study, overseen by Columbia sociology professor C. Wright Mills, compared urban manufacturing areas in the Midwest. It found that locations with many small companies had a more robust economic life, with higher socioeconomic well-being, than areas dominated by a few large firms. Many rural sociologists have tested these findings since then. One, a Cornell study led by rural sociologist Thomas Lyson, found a way to counter the effects of farm consolidation. Using U.S. Census of Agriculture and other county-level data, it found that communities with large-scale industrial-style farms that also had politically active populations and a high percentage of people running small, independent businesses tended to have higher levels of social well-being than those without. The effect of economic concentration Looking at the agriculture sector in 2026, it’s clear that policymakers have not listened to the concerns raised by Berry or the rural sociologists. According to the latest Census of Agriculture, America had fewer than 2 million farms in 2022. Fewer than 6% of those farms accounted for over three-quarters of all agricultural production. Farms are getting larger and more specialized. Economist Jim MacDonald documented that half of all cropland in 2017 was on farms with 1,445 acres, more than double the 650 acres in 1987. Half of all dairy farms had more than 1,300 cows in 2017, up from 80 in 1987. Half of all pig farms in 1987 marketed 1,200 pigs or more – the midpoint is currently over 50,000 pigs per year. The number of American farms fell while the size of those farms grew as consolidation became common across the country in the second half of the 20th century. USDA The supply chain is also shrinking, leaving farmers with fewer choices. Today, fewer companies control more of the markets where farmers buy their fertilizers and pesticides or sell their products, which means that farmers have less control over what they can raise or sell. For instance, just two companies accounted for 71.6% of the U.S. corn seed market in 2018-2022, and those same two companies accounted for 65.9% of the soybean seed market, according to USDA researchers. Twenty years earlier, the top two companies in those markets accounted for 47.2% of the corn seed market and 41.8% of the soybean seed market. When four or fewer firms control 40% or more of a market, farmers tend to pay more for seeds, fertilizer and pest control and receive less for their commodities, while consumers continue to face higher prices. Consolidation of land and commodity markets at the farm level often goes unnoticed and sometimes undocumented. University of Iowa economist Silvia Secchi describes how changes in the U.S. Census of Agriculture in 2002 and in 2017 “obfuscates the degree of consolidation” in the farm sector by allowing farms to report up to three or four farm operators. These changes have led to the official count of over 3 million farm operators, even though there are fewer than 2 million farms. By looking at the volume of sales, Secchi found that fewer than half of these 2 million farms produce commodities worth more than $1,000 annually. She contends that this way of counting farmers does a double disservice to small farm operators. First, it lumps disadvantaged farmers into a group that includes retired farmers and farmland owners who might be using their land as a tax write-off. Second, when the overall farm incomes are averaged, the inclusion of these small farmers make the large, high-value farmers appear to need more federal support. How to improve conditions in farm country Restoring the vibrant rural farm economy of the past may be unrealistic, but some policies could at least improve conditions. Devising new – and enforcing existing – antitrust laws to break up oligopolies and monopolies in the materials farms need, such as seeds and fertilizer, as well as in processing and trade could give farmers more choices about what to raise and where to sell it, while protecting consumers from high prices. Irrigated fields stretch for miles in many rural farming regions across the middle of America, including on Colorado’s eastern plains. Jim Wark /Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Right-to-repair laws could help farmers gain more control over their expensive machinery. Farm subsidies could be directed to smaller farmers who produce food – many of whom were inspired by Berry to become farmers – rather than toward the largest farmers who produce a few commodities at a massive scale. And finally, policymakers can develop rural policies that actually invest in the rural environment and communities, rather than simply subsidizing commodities in ways that primarily benefit the corporate owners of vast areas of farmland. 41496c8a0956b93d: Tech stocks are on a bumpy ride, weighed down by the slump in Nvidia's shares. Liu Yanan/Xinhua via Getty ImagesAfter stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks. Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Here are some basic facts to guide your planning. Many Americans are saving on autopilot Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund, which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund. About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion. Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices: U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund, who expect to retire imminently. The idea of target-date funds is that you can put your retirement savings on autopilot, with the mix of stocks and bonds getting more conservative the older you get. Brano on Unsplash Tech volatility is forcing new questions That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers, Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4%. Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds have significant tech exposure Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold. And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500, according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund, with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average. What to check now if you own a target-date fund In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone. The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. When markets are jumpy, savers should review the funds they hold and consider rebalancing toward lower risk if they’re close to retiring. Towfiqu Barbhuiya on Unsplash, CC BY But a saver still needs to check three things. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. What to do if you hold other funds About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly. For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund, and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. But the pattern can flip quickly: International stocks gained about 29% in 2025, far ahead of the S&P 500’s 16%. Align your savings to your timeline How much this month’s news matters depends on when you’ll need the money. If you’re decades from retirement, a downturn can work in your favor, because every paycheck contribution buys shares at lower prices. Keep contributing and capture your full employer match. My own research with a colleague has found that accounts on systematic investment plans akin to 401(k)s earned better market-adjusted returns than accounts funded with lump sums. If you’re within 5-10 years of retirement, the bigger danger is what planners call sequence-of-returns risk: A large loss right before or just after you start withdrawing can permanently shrink what your savings can support. A good defense is to hold several years of expected withdrawals in lower-risk assets, such as bonds or money market funds, so you’re never forced to sell stocks after a drop. For retirees, Morningstar’s Christine Benz suggests one to two years of withdrawals in cash and five to eight more in bonds. What not to do The costliest mistake is usually the most tempting: selling everything and waiting for the dust to settle. During the 2008-09 financial crisis, about 117,000 Fidelity 401(k) participants moved entirely out of stocks. Those who stayed out saw their balances grow just 2% by mid-2011, while those who kept some stock exposure saw balances rise 50% on average. Other moves to avoid include stopping your own 401(k) contributions, chasing whatever theme looks safe this month, and pulling money out early, which can mean taxes, penalties and a locked-in loss. Last, don’t hand the decision to a chatbot. It will likely give you sound general guidance, such as diversifying and not panic-selling, and that consensus advice is where AI is reliable. But it is weakest on high-stakes questions that turn on your own situation.
