b6a152aa5fb65c1a: The state welcome accorded to French president Emmanuel Macron at Dataran Merdeka on Nov 17 reflected Malaysia’s growing strategic importance to France, a European country that is also an Indo-Pacific power.

France is not merely an external observer of the Indo-Pacific. Through its overseas territories, maritime interests, military presence and extensive exclusive economic zones, France has a permanent stake in the region. Malaysia, meanwhile, occupies one of Asia’s most consequential geographical positions.
It sits between the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, two maritime spaces indispensable to international commerce, energy security and regional stability.
The convergence of French strategic interests and Malaysia’s geographical significance creates opportunities for both countries to deepen their partnership.
France is an Indo-Pacific power

France possesses overseas territories in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, including Réunion, French Polynesia and New Caledonia. These territories give France a permanent population, maritime jurisdiction and security responsibilities across the Indo-Pacific.

Unlike European countries whose regional engagement depends primarily on diplomacy or commercial investment, France maintains a continuous physical presence. Its naval forces, surveillance capabilities and defence partnerships enable Paris to contribute to maritime security across vast distances.
Yet the Indo-Pacific cannot be secured through military deployments alone. The region requires diplomacy, economic connectivity, institutional cooperation and respect for international law.
This is where Malaysia becomes important.
Malaysia’s strategic geography

The Straits of Malacca is among the world’s most important maritime arteries. It connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea and the wider Pacific, facilitating trade between Europe, the Middle East, South Asia and East Asia.
Any serious disruption here would affect shipping costs, energy supplies and global supply chains. Malaysia shares responsibility for the security of this passage with Indonesia and Singapore.

Malaysia is both a maritime trading nation and a claimant state in the South China Sea. Its economic interests depend on freedom of navigation, uninterrupted commercial activity and the peaceful management of maritime disputes.

France therefore has compelling reasons to strengthen relations with Putrajaya. Malaysia offers Paris a diplomatic interlocutor linking the Indian and Pacific Oceans, while France gives Putrajaya another avenue for cooperation without excessive dependence on Washington or Beijing.
Beyond great-power rivalry
Competition between the US and China increasingly shapes the Indo-Pacific. Reducing the region to a binary confrontation, however, would be shortsighted.

France has traditionally emphasised strategic autonomy, even while remaining a member of Nato and a close US ally. Malaysia similarly values strategic independence and constructive relations with competing powers.
Both countries should recognise that smaller and medium-sized powers cannot be expected to surrender their national interests to the preferences of larger states.

Asean must remain central to regional diplomacy. France can support Asean-led institutions, including the East Asia Summit and Asean Regional Forum, while respecting the sovereignty of Southeast Asian countries.
The objective should not be to militarise the Indo-Pacific, but to strengthen a rules-based regional order through dialogue, confidence-building measures and practical cooperation.
Malaysia as a Europe-Asean bridge

This is where Malaysia can assume a more consequential diplomatic role. Its value to France should not be measured only by geography or bilateral trade. Malaysia can also serve as a bridge between European strategic interests and Asean's regional priorities.

Malaysia’s long-standing participation in Asean gives it an understanding of the region’s diplomatic sensitivities and diversity. Since Southeast Asian countries do not always share identical views on major-power competition or maritime disputes, European engagement must be based on consultation and respect for Asean centrality.

France can use its relationship with Malaysia to deepen its engagement with Southeast Asia. Putrajaya can help explain Asean's preference for inclusive dialogue and practical cooperation, while conveying European perspectives to regional partners.
This does not mean Malaysia should speak on behalf of every Asean member. Rather, it can help create channels through which European and Southeast Asian policymakers better understand one another.

The opportunity extends beyond France. As an EU member, France can contribute to stronger Asean-EU relations in maritime cooperation, digital governance, clean energy, education and resilient supply chains. These are areas of shared interest, but cooperation must be shaped around local needs and mutually agreed priorities.

Malaysia’s engagement with the EU provides a foundation. Stronger ties with France can connect governments, universities and businesses, turning diplomatic goodwill into sustained exchanges and practical projects.
A partnership across two strategic seas

Acting as a diplomatic bridge requires Malaysia to preserve its strategic autonomy, maintain constructive relations with major powers and remain committed to Asean-led processes. Its credibility rests on showing that cooperation need not force Southeast Asian countries into rival camps.

For France, this means engaging Malaysia as a partner with its own agency, not simply as a gateway for French influence. For Malaysia, it means widening its diplomatic and economic options while reinforcing Asean voice.

Ultimately, the significance of Macron’s visit should not be measured solely by the agreements announced. Its longer-term importance lies in whether Malaysia and France can build a partnership connecting two strategically important regions.

At the crossroads of the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, Malaysia can do more than safeguard maritime interests: it can help bring Europe and Asean closer through dialogue and practical cooperation.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
669406732a3f4212: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
f4cc3245def3a5b6: Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim's statement following his audience with Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir should put to rest any uncertainties and mark the end of a protracted crisis.

Ismail has made it clear that he will abide by the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang decisions and procedures in all matters concerning customs and administration. Party politics should have no place in such matters.
However, the end of this constitutional crisis may spark another - one that concerns not only the people of Negeri Sembilan but the entire country.
A crisis of integrity involving Umno’s top leadership, particularly those who also hold senior positions in Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Cabinet.
A setback that could lead to public calls for Umno to quit the government for attempting to remove a legitimate and just state ruler.
(Calls that could easily drown out chants of "bubar" (dissolve Parliament) that were heard following Umno's convincing victory in the Melaka state election.)
To re-cap, Ismail has denied submitting or agreeing to a resignation letter as menteri besar, contrary to what was announced by Barisan Nasional secretary-general Zambry Abdul Kadir.

His denial raises serious questions. Why was the letter made public? Who prepared it, and on whose authority was it submitted? Why did the process appear to move ahead without first obtaining the Yang Dipertuan Besar’s consent?
These questions should not be directed at Zambry, who is also the higher education minister, alone.
Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who is also the deputy prime minister, has also offered an explanation that now appears to contradict Ismail’s own account.
Now, if Zahid and Zambry only held posts in Umno, this controversy could be easily reduced to internal strife within the party or dismissed as another political dispute in Negeri Sembilan.
But they don't.
Which is why any reservations about their honesty, transparency and credibility cannot be taken lightly.
There are three key questions that need to be answered.
First, who actually prepared the resignation letter for Ismail that Zambry announced?
Second, did Ismail really not provide any reason for supposedly stepping down as menteri besar as Zahid claimed?
Or was this simply a tragic case of a misunderstanding or misinformation?

Third, why did Zahid and Umno submit a candidate for the menteri besar's post to the state ruler, following Ismail's resignation, despite Tuanku Muhriz allowing the Juasseh assemblyman to continue in his role?
I sincerely hope Zambry and Zahid will provide clear, comprehensive and convincing answers to all three questions.
Such explanations are important, not just to protect their reputations, but also to restore public confidence in the integrity of leaders entrusted with governing the country.
I still want to believe that there are capable Malay leaders whom the people can rely on. Leaders who also respect the royal institution, the Malay rulers, and the constitution.
But political statements alone won't win new converts or retain the current devotees. Instilling such belief requires honest and responsible action.

In examining the Negeri Sembilan crisis, another question deserves closer attention. Was everything that happened part of a deliberate plan, or was it simply the result of misunderstandings and poor communication among those involved?
If it was merely a misunderstanding, a sincere explanation and an apology should be enough for everyone to move forward.
But if the crisis is proven to have been orchestrated, whether by political figures, customary authorities or both, the consequences would go far beyond a power struggle in a single state.
It could undermine public confidence in customary institutions, the supremacy of the constitution, and the integrity of a Malay party with a long history in the formation of this nation.

Politicians should remember that in today's world, backroom dealings are harder to conceal, thanks to social media. A seemingly innocuous remark by a lowly clerk could create a butterfly effect that threatens a powerful party leader.
Once trust erodes, even loyal supporters may become disillusioned, while political allies may choose to distance themselves.
This is why integrity cannot be an afterthought in politicking.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
73927cb8c81d9316: Kenyataan Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan Ismail Lasim selepas menghadap Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir semalam, pada hemat saya, menandakan berakhirnya kemelut yang mencetuskan persoalan mengenai kedudukan pemerintah negeri serta keabsahan pelantikan Undang.

Ismail dengan jelas menyatakan pendiriannya untuk akur kepada keputusan dan tatakelola Dewan Keadilan dan Undang dalam segala urusan berkaitan adat dan pentadbiran. Politik kepartian pula tidak seharusnya mencampuri urusan berkenaan.
Alhamdulillah, sebagai rakyat yang mengikuti perkembangan ini, saya bersyukur kerana kebenaran akhirnya mendapat tempat, sekali gus meredakan kekeliruan yang sekian lama menyelubungi Negeri Sembilan.
Namun, berakhirnya kemelut perlembagaan ini membuka satu lagi persoalan yang tidak kurang serius, bukan sahaja kepada rakyat Negeri Sembilan, malah seluruh negara.
Persoalan itu menyentuh integriti pucuk pimpinan Umno, khususnya mereka yang turut memegang jawatan penting dalam Kabinet Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim.

Jika sebelum ini kedengaran laungan 'bubar, bubar' selepas kemenangan besar pada PRN Melaka, jangan sampai rakyat pula mula melaungkan 'keluar, keluar' terhadap Umno apabila integriti kepimpinannya dipersoalkan susulan kemelut yang turut dikaitkan dengan usaha menyingkirkan pemerintah negeri yang sah selain memerintah dengan baik, adil serta saksama.
Lebih membimbangkan, persoalan ini timbul daripada kenyataan Ismail sendiri, bukannya khabar angin atau dakwaan pihak ketiga.

Ismail secara terbuka menafikan beliau pernah menghantar atau memberikan persetujuan terhadap surat peletakan jawatan sebagai menteri besar yang diumumkan Setiausaha Agung Barisan Nasional (BN) Zambry Abdul Kadir.

Penafian itu menimbulkan persoalan besar. Mengapa surat berkenaan diumumkan kepada umum? Siapa yang menyediakannya dan atas kuasa siapa ia dikemukakan? Mengapa pula proses itu seolah-olah mendahului perkenan Yang DiPertuan Besar?
Persoalan ini tidak wajar dipertanggungjawabkan hanya kepada Zambry yang juga menteri pendidikan tinggi.
Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi yang juga timbalan perdana menteri, turut memberikan penjelasan yang kini menimbulkan percanggahan dengan pendirian Ismail sendiri.
Sekiranya kedua-dua pemimpin itu sekadar memegang jawatan dalam Umno, mungkin kemelut ini boleh dianggap sebagai masalah dalaman parti atau isu politik Negeri Sembilan semata-mata.
Namun, hakikatnya kedua-duanya memegang amanah besar dalam pentadbiran negara. Justeru, sebarang persoalan mengenai kejujuran, ketelusan dan kewibawaan mereka tidak boleh dipandang ringan.
Sebagai rakyat Malaysia, saya mempunyai rasa hormat terhadap kedua-dua tokoh ini. Namun, perkembangan terbaharu menyebabkan saya tertanya-tanya tentang kewajaran tindakan dan penjelasan mereka.
Ada tiga persoalan utama yang perlu dijawab secara terbuka.
Pertama, siapakah sebenarnya yang menulis atau menyediakan surat peletakan jawatan Ismail yang diumumkan Zambry?

Kedua, benarkah penjelasan Zahid bahawa Ismail tidak memberikan sebarang alasan kepadanya berhubung peletakan jawatan itu? Atau adakah penjelasan tersebut berpunca daripada salah faham atau maklumat yang tidak tepat?

Ketiga, mengapakah Zahid dan Umno masih mengemukakan nama calon menteri besar baharu untuk perkenan Tuanku Muhriz, sedangkan terdapat kenyataan bahawa baginda memperkenankan Ismail meneruskan tugasnya?
Saya amat berharap Zambry dan Zahid dapat memberikan penjelasan yang jelas, menyeluruh dan meyakinkan terhadap ketiga-tiga persoalan ini.
Penjelasan itu penting bukan semata-mata untuk mempertahankan nama baik mereka, tetapi juga bagi memulihkan keyakinan rakyat terhadap integriti pemimpin yang diberikan amanah untuk mentadbir negara.
Saya masih mahu percaya bahawa orang Melayu mempunyai pemimpin berwibawa yang mampu menjadi tempat rakyat bersandar, selain menghormati institusi Raja-raja Melayu dan prinsip perlembagaan.
Namun, kepercayaan itu tidak boleh dipertahankan dengan kenyataan politik semata-mata. Ia mesti disokong oleh tindakan yang jujur dan bertanggungjawab.

Dalam menilai kemelut Negeri Sembilan ini, satu lagi persoalan perlu diperhalusi. Adakah segala yang berlaku berpunca daripada perancangan tertentu, atau sekadar salah faham dan kegagalan komunikasi antara pihak berkepentingan?
Jika benar ia hanya salah faham, penjelasan yang ikhlas dan permohonan maaf sepatutnya memadai untuk membolehkan semua pihak bergerak ke hadapan.
Tetapi jika terbukti kemelut ini dirancang, sama ada oleh pihak politik, pihak adat atau kedua-duanya, kesannya jauh lebih besar daripada sekadar perebutan kuasa di sebuah negeri.
Ia boleh meruntuhkan keyakinan rakyat terhadap institusi adat, keluhuran perlembagaan dan integriti sebuah parti Melayu yang mempunyai sejarah panjang dalam pembentukan negara.
Saya ingin mengingatkan ahli politik semua bahawa this is a different age altogether. Perbuatan tersembunyi sukar ditutup dengan kewujudan media sosial dan maklumat digital.
Maklumat daripada seorang kerani sekalipun boleh membuka ruang kepada pendedahan yang akhirnya menggugat kedudukan pemimpin besar sesebuah parti.
Apabila kepercayaan mula terhakis, penyokong sendiri boleh menjadi serik, manakala rakan politik pula mungkin memilih untuk menjauhkan diri.
Sebab itulah integriti tidak boleh dianggap sebagai perkara sampingan dalam percaturan politik. Ia merupakan asas kepercayaan rakyat terhadap seseorang pemimpin.

Kalau nak 'bubar-bubar' lebih baik 'keluar-keluar' kerana kami perlukan pemimpin yang boleh dipercayai dan berintegriti kepada sumpah khidmat kepada rakyat semua dan sumpah ketaatan kepada Raja Melayu.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
b894a0e31143a149: When Southeast Asia’s leaders link arms for their customary family photo at the Asean Summit in Manila on Nov 16–18, the show of unity will belie the fact that, on the eve of the organisation’s 60th anniversary, the group is more divided and less effective than ever.
Amid a fracturing global order, Asean has a choice: turn its convening authority into concerted action or be reduced to an arena for great-power rivalry.
The fault lines are numerous. Indonesia’s wildfire haze has choked Singapore and Malaysia in recent months. Thailand and Cambodia fought border skirmishes that came close to outright war last year.

Myanmar is led by a putschist-turned-president who wants his seat back at the leaders’ table. And the Philippines, the summit’s host, is locked in a standoff with China that most of its neighbours would rather avoid.
And yet Southeast Asia needs Asean more than ever because it gives member countries visibility and a voice on the global stage.

To be sure, Asean is not in danger of collapse. The risk is subtler. Each fissure exposes an institutional shortcoming. On Myanmar, it is enforcement: Min Aung Hlaing, the general who ousted and detained the democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021, signed Asean’s Five-Point Consensus in April of that year, only to disregard it. The group responded by barring the junta leader from attending Asean summits.

But after winning Myanmar’s military-organised elections—with voting confined to junta-controlled areas, excluding large swaths of the country—in December and January, Min Aung Hlaing swapped his general’s uniform for civilian garb in April.
Hard-headed realpolitik compelled China and India to recognise him, while half of Asean members, led by Thailand, have also now officially received him, amounting to de facto normalisation.
Likewise, the Thai-Cambodian conflict exposed the limits of Asean’s much-touted capacity to sustain peace. Fighting in July 2025 killed dozens and displaced some 300,000 people.

The first ceasefire came after US president Donald Trump threatened tariffs, leading to the “truce for trade” accord signed in October 2025. But it unraveled only a couple months later, with border clashes uprooting many more people.

Without pressure from the US, Asean could not end the fighting on its own. Both sides are now using the “compulsory conciliation” process under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea to resolve their bilateral conflict.

Meanwhile, tensions in the South China Sea reveal the absence of common external positions in Asean. China exploits member states’ differing views of it to pursue its maritime claims, leaving the Philippines exposed, particularly given America’s unpredictability under Trump.

The Philippines wants to complete a long-promised code of conduct for the South China Sea at this month’s summit. But even if the code is finalised, a text without teeth will not do much to stop China’s incursions.

Indonesian peatland fires have exposed the most telling rift, because great powers play no part in it. The haze closed schools in Malaysia and resulted in Singapore’s longest period of toxic air since 2015, triggering consumer boycotts, ministerial barbs, and a reduction in Indonesia’s pipeline gas exports to Singapore.
But Indonesia alone cannot address the problem. The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution has been in force since 2003, yet its 2020 target for a smoke-free region was pushed back to 2030.

Singapore has issued notices to ten locally-based companies over their links to the fires causing the current haze. A treaty that fails to reach those boardrooms will do little to protect the region’s people from hazardous smoke.

These fault lines matter more than ever because the US-China contest has turned coercive, with tariffs, export controls, critical minerals, and supply chains wielded as weapons, at the same time as the multilateralism that once cushioned smaller countries is being eroded.

Here Asean’s value as a buffer, bridge, and broker is easily overlooked. Despite lacking a unified foreign policy and a joint military, Asean serves as a single interlocutor representing nearly 700 million people and some US$4 trillion in output. It also brings together the US, China, Russia, Japan, India, and others at its East Asia Summit and related forums.

While leaders call for like-minded countries to form coalitions of the willing amid a “rupture” in the global order, Asean member states have already started hedging: Indonesia is now a full member of BRICS, while Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam are partner countries. But these countries need an anchor at home, lest diversification turns into fragmentation. The task now is to demonstrate Asean’s centrality.
Singapore’s 2027 chairmanship offers an opening for several major reforms. Asean should hold fewer summits, with one leaders’ meeting per year and ministers held responsible for delivery.
The group also should hire a secretary-general based on merit and for shorter, performance-dependent contracts, rather than appointing someone for a five-year term, based on alphabetical rotation.

And flexible participation should be the norm, extending the “Asean Minus X” formula used for economic integration to coalitions of the willing on issues such as maritime security, haze enforcement, and scam centres.
Asean would also benefit from empowering past, present, and incoming chairs to mediate conflicts, advance existing agreements, and launch new initiatives.

Lastly, Myanmar’s return to the leaders’ summit should be tied to measurable benchmarks, such as an end to air strikes on civilians, humanitarian access, the release of political prisoners including Aung San Suu Kyi, and an envoy acceptable to all sides.

The aim is not to turn Asean into a supranational authority or geopolitical bloc, but to recover the founding aspiration of 1967, when five wary neighbours judged their quarrels less dangerous than facing outside pressure alone.

Their number has since grown to 11, and member states must remember that endurance does not amount to agency; the choice now is between strengthening their partnership or being picked apart one by one.
Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a professor at Chulalongkorn University’s Faculty of Political Science, is a senior fellow at its Institute of Security and International Studies.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
ce0911f5eee0ae94: From Moaz Nair

Fresh off a string of dominant state election victories in 2026, Barisan Nasional (BN) finds itself in the enviable position of having the political upper hand ahead of the 16th general election (GE16).

Yet, as attention shifts from state assemblies to the battle for Putrajaya, a critical question looms over the nation's political landscape: can BN and Perikatan Nasional (PN) successfully divide parliamentary seats for GE16, or will irreconcilable demands push BN back into the arms of Pakatan Harapan (PH)?
On paper, a BN-PN federal pact appears to be the logical next step.
The two coalitions recently demonstrated the potency of their combined Malay-majority appeal by sweeping the Negeri Sembilan and Melaka state elections on Aug 1 and Nov 14.

However, just a day after the Melaka victory, BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi poured cold water on assumptions of an automatic federal alliance, saying BN has no current plans to extend its state-level cooperation with PN to GE16.
Behind Zahid’s caution lies a mathematical and territorial impasse that threatens to derail parliamentary seat negotiations before they even begin.

The primary obstacle is the clash over seat allocation formulas. According to political analysts, PAS-led PN is expected to insist on an "incumbency formula", whereby each party defends the parliamentary seats it won in the 2022 general election (GE15).
While such a rule sounds straightforward, it would be devastating for BN. In GE15, PN captured 73 federal seats compared to BN’s 30.

Accepting incumbency as the baseline would force Umno to surrender dozens of its traditional Malay-majority constituencies across Perak, Pahang, Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan, Terengganu, Selangor and Melaka.

Early friction is already visible on the ground. In Perak’s Padang Rengas constituency, former four-term Umno MP Nazri Aziz signalled his desire to reclaim the seat, only for incumbent PN MP Azahari Hasan to publicly rule out stepping aside.
Multiply that dispute across 40 or 50 rural constituencies, and the fragility of a BN-PN federal pact becomes immediately clear.

Furthermore, BN enters these negotiations with vastly different leverage than it had in 2022. A solo landslide victory in Johor in July 2026 – where BN won 48 of 56 state seats while PN was completely wiped out with just 5.45% of the popular vote – proved that Umno has regained significant strength in the south.

In Johor, where BN holds nine parliamentary seats to PN’s two, BN has strong grounds to demand the lion's share of the state's 26 federal seats. At the same time, internal pressure within both coalitions leaves little room for compromise.

BN components like MIC have urged the leadership to abandon strict incumbency rules so that non-Umno partners are not sidelined, while BN reportedly aims to contest at least 115 federal seats to lead the next federal government.
If PN refuses to accommodate BN’s demand for more parliamentary seats, Zahid has ensured that he has an escape route: continuing or deepening his coalition's cooperation with PH.

From a purely territorial standpoint, a BN-PH electoral pact offers far less friction than a deal with PN. Because PH’s electoral strength is concentrated in urban and mixed-ethnic constituencies, there is minimal overlap with Umno's rural Malay heartland seats.

Rather than fighting over the same traditional Malay constituencies, BN and PH could divide the electoral map along geographic and demographic lines, allowing BN to contest the large slate of rural seats it desires without yielding ground to PAS and its allies.

Additionally, BN and PH already share an established working relationship as formal partners in the federal unity government, a tie Zahid notably reaffirmed even while celebrating BN’s victory with PN in Melaka.
Beyond coalition deals, BN’s dominant solo performance in Johor leaves open the possibility of contesting GE16 independently in select regions without fielding candidates in all 222 seats.

However, pivoting back to PH carries severe electoral risks for BN. The primary motivation behind BN’s state-level cooperation with PN was to eliminate three-cornered fights and prevent the splitting of Malay votes.
Walking away from PN to align with PH in GE16 would almost certainly trigger fierce three-way battles across Peninsular Malaysia, allowing PH to capitalise on divided Malay support.

Moreover, constantly shifting between PH and PN could create the perception that Umno prioritises short-term seat calculations over a consistent ideological direction, especially as identity-based politics recently favoured the BN-PN formula in peninsula state polls.

When weighing these competing realities, the most probable outcome is that BN will ultimately return to cooperating with PH for GE16 – or pursue a hybrid strategy anchored by a PH pact – rather than forge a full federal alliance with PN.
For Umno, politics is fundamentally about survival and relevance, and a coalition deal that locks it out of dozens of its traditional Malay heartland seats is a non-starter.

PAS and its allies have little incentive to surrender hard-won parliamentary constituencies to revive their chief rival for the Malay vote, making a comprehensive BN-PN seat compromise virtually impossible.
By contrast, PH offers BN the exact political oxygen it needs: a clear, uncontested runway to rebuild in rural Malay constituencies while PH secures urban and mixed seats.

While returning to PH risks splitting the Malay vote, BN’s commanding 2026 state victories suggest it now possesses the momentum to weather three-cornered fights – something it could never achieve while confined to the junior-partner status PN would inevitably impose.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
b25faad8ca59e1f2: The party out of power tends to do well in American midterm elections, and the recent vote was no exception. But what happened this month in the US was something more. Much more.

The vote giving Democrats firm control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives was, first and foremost, a rebuke to President Donald Trump and what he has wrought in his second term: higher prices owing to tariffs and the Iran war, unprecedented corruption, and cruelty towards immigrants.

Trump increasingly seemed out of touch, focussing on his vanity projects—the White House ballroom, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, an “Arc d’Trump” overlooking Arlington National Cemetery—rather than the concerns of everyday Americans. Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot, and they did.

Trump was not the only loser. Elon Musk spent nearly a half-billion dollars with nothing to show for it. Republicans at the state level who pushed for redrawing congressional districts to favour their party came up short. So, too, did the technology companies wanting to build new data centres to power their AI efforts.

Israel will have to contend with a Congress less supportive and less likely to look away from what it is doing in Gaza and the West Bank. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also lost: overnight, his ties to Trump became more of a liability than an asset.

As for the winners, I would begin with the country, in the sense that the blowout spared Americans the prolonged political crisis that could have followed a close election whose results were not accepted.
The country also won in a larger sense: The revival of competitive two-party politics will force politicians to pay attention to the centre and not just their respective extremes.

The Democrats came out on top in the midterms by staying on message and focussing on affordability. But, from voters’ perspective, there is an enormous difference between repudiating the administration and embracing the alternative.
Winning big by itself does not signify a mandate, which requires running on a specific set of policies that are endorsed by a majority of those voting.

The Democrats did not do this for the most part. Affordability is not a policy. Nor is anti-corruption. What they did (correctly) was field a number of appealing candidates and focus on the high cost of living, the self-enrichment of Trump and his inner circle, and the cruelty of mass deportations.

The danger is that many Democrats will now overreach, claiming a mandate when one doesn’t exist. In the process, they could make themselves the issue—by, say, calling for excessive taxation, restoring diversity requirements, or again weakening border controls—rather than focus on measures that are both doable and desirable.
The new congressional leadership has its work cut out for it, although the scale of the Democrats’ victory helps, because it weakens the leverage of the party’s left wing.
As for the Republicans, the danger is that they ignore the message of the electorate. Trump, for his part, seems to have been thrown off balance by the scale of the defeat.
He has already taken it out on chief of staff Susie Wiles (who resigned) and replaced her with Stephen Miller, the architect of a presidency defined by executive orders and mass deportations.
And then Trump posted that the vote was rigged. The good news is that this totally unsubstantiated claim generated more pushback than traction.

In the longer run, the midterm results open up the 2028 race to succeed Trump. Vice-president JD Vance, until recently the frontrunner, has the advantage of opposing the Iran war, but carries the considerable baggage of close association with Trump.

Distancing himself from Trump without alienating him promises to be a never-ending ordeal. I expect the changed map—Texas and even Florida are now in play, and the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin are governed by Democrats—to make the Democratic presidential nomination even more competitive. Well over a dozen candidates could decide to dip their toes in the water.

There will be time for all that. For now, the American people are looking for relief on gasoline, food, electricity, housing, and healthcare costs. Rolling back unwarranted tariffs, reclaiming authority over them, makes sense. Providing economic and military help to Ukraine ought to be on the agenda as well.
All of this will take legislation, ideally passed with support from Republicans who may see advantage in being viewed as willing to work across the aisle.

Achieving lower prices will also require ending the Iran war. The challenge will be doing so on terms the US government can live with when it comes to reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ensuring that Iran does not develop nuclear weapons. The answer is not to be found in a new round of military strikes that would risk calamitous escalation without promising constructive results.

There will be little the Democrats can do to influence all this. US presidents control most of the power when it comes to American foreign policy and the use of military force. It will be up to Trump to decide next steps towards Iran.

As a lame-duck president, Trump, eager to remind the country and the world that he is still in charge, might double down on his ill-advised war of choice. But so far, at least, his statements suggest otherwise.

The problem is that ending the war will require cooperation by Iran, whose leaders may well see the results of the midterms as giving them reason to press for more concessions from a weakened Trump. The US overreached when it launched the war, but Iran may succumb to the same temptation now.
Richard Haass, president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, is a senior counselor at Centerview Partners and distinguished university scholar at New York University.

33a61caea8aae9aa: Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples. Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview. Q: What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?    A: This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.  As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact. I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better. Q: Can you walk us through how the project has evolved? A: When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved. Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example. Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques. Q: What would you say are some recent highlights of your work? A: Our IPLoc research was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context. Then, we had an audio-based paper, OmniR1, that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are multiple-choice answers. A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks. We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior. Q: Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data? A: These days, we can't create one of these very large foundation models ourselves. We don't have the resources to do that, so we're tending to use these available models and trying to adapt them, train them in a weakly supervised way, methods that don't require as much data, like our work on test-time reinforcement learning. Our project was not monolithic, in the sense that we're not all working on one thing. It's more like a thousand flowers bloom, so there's no one particular way that we're approaching things. Q: In the near future, how do you see multimodal research evolving in your MIT-IBM research team? A: Over the years, we probably produced two dozen or so significant collaborative papers, and during this work, it was amazing to me that the machines could learn these correspondences without being told anything. No one had ever shown that machines could do it before we did that. Some of our early work combining audio with large language models was fun, too: seeing the model talk about what it heard and then having a conversation with it. Now, we are starting to take this for granted, but at the time, it was fun to see. Moving forward, for the coming year, with our MIT-IBM collaboration, we're going to switch gears a little bit and focus more on what's known as full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. These are models that are listening while they’re talking, so it’s more like how humans operate, and this is quite different from what we’ve been doing up until now, which is joint audio-visual work, which we will also continue.  Now, we’ll be focusing on the speech side of things. These full-duplex models have suddenly become an interesting thing to look at, because they would move you away from the rigid turn-taking approach that is used right now when you're talking to some of these models. Ultimately, I think they will be more natural to interact with.  These full-duplex models are just starting to emerge, and some of the ones that are publicly available aren't as good as the big, large language models. They can handle some of these low-level communication skills, but they're still missing some things, like the concept of time, or knowledge depth. So, we're working on trying to address some of these issues. This research has been conducted in coordination with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab teams of Rogerio Feris, Brian Kingsbury, and Samuel Thomas of IBM Research, and Hilde Kuehne of the University of Tuebingen, who is an MIT-IBM affiliated researcher.
6e086317ffb3ab4e: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.
480a8b723958aa8d: Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time. Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.  “Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.” Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult.  “Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world. “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS. “A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems. “It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?” “We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos. Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says. To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.” He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.” The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions. Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.” “AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.” The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.” “The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is now accessible online at PNAS. A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award. “Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”
c4fcf3d7ab6e8c9f: A 'Saturday Night Live' parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem. Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people. The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. A growing trend One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion. The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving. Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460. But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members. NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores. Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.
